title: Not All Agreement Counts as Corroboration: Provenance-Conserving Multi-View Fusion for Typed Action Admission in Human-Robot Collaboration
comment: 35 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables. Code and supporting materials: https://github.com/ZekaiJ/PACT
summary: For embodied systems, predictive agreement alone does not determine whether evidence warrants action; evidential origin matters. Repeated inference over one observation can multiply agreement without adding evidence, while source-local values do not reveal whether outputs have separately countable origins. PACT treats evidence countability as a relational variable for provenance-conserving fusion and typed action admission. A supplied provenance partition defines countable units. PACT retains coordinatewise support shared within each unit, accumulates only across units, and maps unmet release conditions to hold, confirm, or fallback. Under the stated assumptions, source-local values cannot identify countability; the coordinatewise meet is the greatest budget satisfying singleton fidelity and insertion non-amplification, with coarsening monotonicity and fixed-partition stability. Across 31,200 evaluations in 48 scene clusters, PACT attains a common-support normalized risk-coverage area (ncsAURC) of 0.0861. Excluding the constructed adversarial-consensus arm, provenance-partition aggregation reduces ncsAURC by 0.0557 relative to singleton aggregation, while the corroboration contrast vanishes. On complete-source records, native scores favor PACT, but a common posterior-peak score narrows its difference from nested Dirichlet and favors product fusion. Reassigning provenance over unchanged predictions moves evidence budgets as predicted. In offline human-robot collaboration, eightfold within-camera duplication leaves 720 typed responses per checkpoint unchanged; camera-grouped PACT admits 47 of 57 Qwen3-VL-32B reference-consistent candidates with no observed reference-inconsistent admission in 60 episodes. PACT separates computational from evidential multiplicity: agreement constitutes corroboration only when provenance permits separate accumulation.

AI.tldr: PACT introduces evidential countability as a relational variable for provenance-conserving fusion in embodied systems, treating agreement as corroboration only when provenance permits separate accumulation. It demonstrates that source-local values cannot identify countability and validates its approach across 31,200 evaluations and offline human-robot collaboration tasks.
AI.motivation: For embodied systems, predictive agreement alone is insufficient for warranting action—evidential origin matters. Repeated inference over a single observation can inflate agreement without adding evidence, and source-local values fail to reveal whether outputs originate separately. The paper addresses the need to distinguish computational multiplicity from evidential multiplicity in decision-making.
AI.method: PACT defines provenance-partition-based countability, retaining coordinatewise support within each provenance unit while accumulating only across distinct units. It uses the coordinatewise meet as the budget for fusion (satisfying singleton fidelity and insertion non-amplification), and maps unmet release conditions to hold, confirm, or fallback actions. Provenance reassignment moves evidence budgets as predicted.
AI.result: Across 48 scene clusters (31,200 evaluations), PACT achieves ncsAURC of 0.0861. Provenance-partition aggregation reduces ncsAURC by 0.0557 versus singleton aggregation (excluding adversarial-consensus arm). In human-robot collaboration, camera-grouped PACT admits 47/57 reference-consistent Qwen3-VL-32B candidates with zero reference-inconsistent admissions across 60 episodes despite eightfold within-camera duplication.
AI.conclusion: PACT separates computational from evidential multiplicity, establishing that agreement constitutes genuine corroboration only when provenance permits separate accumulation. Provenance is a critical relational dimension for evidence counting that source-local values cannot recover.

title: TriSAR: Task Coordination and Collision Avoidance for Aerial Robot Teams in Disaster Response
summary: Multi-Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) disaster-response systems require coordinated task assignment and local trajectory control, yet the individual and combined contributions of these coordination layers to mission efficiency and operational safety remain insufficiently characterised under controlled experimental conditions. TriSAR is evaluated as a five-UAV coordination system operating in a physics-based Gazebo simulation of an earthquake-damaged urban environment. A 2 x 2 factorial design compares two task-allocation strategies (Genetic Algorithm and greedy fitness-based allocation) with reactive collision avoidance enabled or disabled. Each of the four configurations was evaluated over 30 stochastic episodes in a common scenario of five UAVs and eight targets. Under greedy allocation, enabling repulsion eliminated recorded collision-threshold violations, confirmed by a Mann-Whitney test (U = 885, p = 4.03 x 10^-12, rank-biserial r = 0.97). Under GA allocation, the same protective effect was confirmed (U = 675, p = 1.26 x 10^-5, rank-biserial r = 0.50). For mission-efficiency metrics, GA-based allocation showed no statistically detectable advantage over greedy allocation when repulsion was enabled, but a significant advantage in steps, path length, and energy when repulsion was disabled (Welch's t-tests, |g| between 0.92 and 1.76). These results show that reactive repulsion provides a substantial, allocation-dependent safety benefit, while the additional computational complexity of GA-based task allocation yields a detectable mission-efficiency benefit only when repulsion is disabled.

AI.tldr: TriSAR, a five-UAV coordination system for disaster response, is evaluated in a Gazebo-based earthquake scenario using a 2×2 factorial design (GA vs. greedy task allocation × reactive repulsion on/off). Reactive repulsion virtually eliminates collision violations regardless of allocation strategy (significant, large-effect Mann-Whitney results), while GA-based allocation only shows significant mission-efficiency advantages (steps, path length, energy) when repulsion is disabled.
AI.motivation: Multi-UAV disaster-response systems rely on both task assignment and local trajectory control, but the independent and combined contributions of each coordination layer to operational safety and mission efficiency have not been rigorously characterized under controlled experimental conditions.
AI.method: A five-UAV system (TriSAR) is tested in a physics-based Gazebo simulation of an earthquake-damaged urban environment. A 2×2 factorial design crosses two task-allocation strategies (Genetic Algorithm vs. greedy fitness-based) with reactive collision avoidance (repulsion) enabled or disabled. Each of the four configurations is run over 30 stochastic episodes with five UAVs and eight targets. Statistical analyses include Mann-Whitney tests for collision violations and Welch's t-tests for mission-efficiency metrics.
AI.result: Enabling repulsion eliminated collision-threshold violations under greedy allocation (U = 885, p = 4.03×10⁻¹², r = 0.97) and under GA allocation (U = 675, p = 1.26×10⁻⁵, r = 0.50). GA-based allocation showed no statistically detectable mission-efficiency advantage over greedy allocation when repulsion was enabled, but showed significant advantages in steps, path length, and energy when repulsion was disabled (Welch's t-tests, |g| between 0.92 and 1.76).
AI.conclusion: Reactive repulsion provides a substantial, allocation-dependent safety benefit, essentially eliminating collision violations. The computational cost of GA-based task allocation only yields a measurable mission-efficiency payoff when reactive collision avoidance is disabled, suggesting that the value of sophisticated allocation strategies depends critically on the presence of lower-level safety mechanisms.

title: Designing Versatile Samples for Learned Trajectory Scoring
summary: Many current end-to-end driving policies emit a pool of candidate trajectories and select one, which makes selection a separable component: a scorer can be retrained while the planner, its backbone, and its trajectory generator all stay frozen. However, many strong planners concentrate their proposals around safe mode, providing limited supervision near decision boundaries. In this work, we design a training dataset that provides more informative supervision for the scorer. In particular, we construct two generators that perturb the logged human trajectory along the two axes a vehicle can be displaced: laterally toward the drivable boundary and longitudinally toward a leading vehicle. The designed dataset produces more informative positive and negative samples than the base planner's proposal pool. We attach a transformer-based scorer to two frozen generative planners, DiffusionDrive and MeanFuser, and train it on the NAVSIM navtrain dataset. The results of the experiments show that we achieve 90.1 EPDMS on DiffusionDrive and 90.4 EPDMS on MeanFuser when using ResNet-34, with 0.4 and 0.3 EPDMS respectively, from the designed training dataset.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to improve trajectory scoring in end-to-end driving by constructing a training dataset with more informative supervision. Two generators perturb logged human trajectories laterally (toward drivable boundaries) and longitudinally (toward leading vehicles) to create positive and negative samples near decision boundaries. A transformer-based scorer attached to frozen planners (DiffusionDrive and MeanFuser) achieves 90.1 and 90.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navtrain, improvements of 0.4 and 0.3 EPDMS respectively.
AI.motivation: End-to-end driving policies select from candidate trajectories via a scorer, which can be trained separately from the frozen planner. However, strong planners concentrate proposals around safe modes, providing limited supervision near decision boundaries where the scorer needs to make critical distinctions.
AI.method: The authors design two generators that create more informative training samples by perturbing logged human trajectories along two axes: laterally toward the drivable boundary and longitudinally toward a leading vehicle. This produces better positive and negative samples than the base planner's proposal pool. A transformer-based scorer is trained on this dataset and attached to two frozen generative planners (DiffusionDrive and MeanFuser) evaluated on NAVSIM navtrain.
AI.result: The method achieves 90.1 EPDMS on DiffusionDrive and 90.4 EPDMS on MeanFuser using ResNet-34, with gains of 0.4 and 0.3 EPDMS respectively over baseline training approaches.
AI.conclusion: Constructing a training dataset with perturbations that expose the scorer to decision-boundary cases—rather than relying solely on the planner's safe-mode proposals—improves trajectory scoring performance in end-to-end driving systems.

title: One Demonstration, Many Objects: Generalizing Manipulation via Local Contact Geometry
summary: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered robot hands promises human-level dexterity, but collecting large-scale dexterous robot hand data remains difficult. Learning from human demonstrations has emerged as a scalable alternative to robot teleoperation, providing strong priors on object interaction and contact strategies. Recent sim-to-real RL methods incorporate such priors, but often (i) omit rewards that explicitly incentivize precise contact, yielding weak real-world performance, and/or (ii) generalize poorly to unseen object instances. We propose DemoMimic (Dexterous Motion Mimic), a policy that manipulates objects by focusing on their geometry local to the contact points. Its contact-centric rewards encourage precise contact and improve sim-to-real consistency, yielding a single real-world policy that transfers across objects of varying shape, scale, mass, and friction wherever local contact structure is preserved. Real-world ablations show that DemoMimic achieves 71% success across 16 objects, four tasks, and two robot-hand embodiments, with the smallest sim-to-real drop compared to baselines.

AI.tldr: DemoMimic is a contact-centric robotic manipulation policy that leverages human demonstrations and explicit contact-based rewards to achieve sim-to-real transfer across diverse objects and robot hand embodiments, reaching 71% real-world success across 16 objects and 4 tasks with minimal sim-to-real performance drop.
AI.motivation: Large-scale data collection for dexterous multi-fingered robot manipulation is difficult. Learning from human demonstrations provides scalable alternatives with strong priors, but existing sim-to-real RL methods either lack rewards that explicitly incentivize precise contact (hurting real-world performance) or generalize poorly to unseen object instances.
AI.method: DemoMimic manipulates objects by focusing on object geometry local to contact points. It uses contact-centric reward functions that incentivize precise contact and improve sim-to-real consistency, resulting in a single policy that transfers across objects with varying shape, scale, mass, and friction where local contact structure is preserved.
AI.result: Real-world ablations show DemoMimic achieves 71% success across 16 objects, four tasks, and two robot-hand embodiments, with the smallest sim-to-real performance drop compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Contact-centric rewards grounded in local object geometry are key to achieving robust sim-to-real transfer in dexterous manipulation, enabling a single policy to generalize across heterogeneous object instances and robot hands.

title: EvalDetectBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Evaluation Awareness in Frontier Language Models
summary: Frontier large language models can often recognize when they are being evaluated, a capability known as evaluation awareness. If models behave differently in evaluations than in deployment, this undermines the validity of evaluation results, which are a crucial component of current AI safety frameworks. We introduce EvalDetectBench, an open pipeline and benchmark for measuring evaluation awareness that works with any Inspect-compatible evaluation, allowing practitioners to test against current and future benchmarks. EvalDetectBench ships with a newly curated transcript suite covering current frontier system-card evaluations and diverse deployment sources. The benchmark serves two purposes: measuring how reliably frontier LLMs recognize that they are being evaluated, and assessing how detectable individual benchmarks are as evaluations. We identify two methodological choices in the existing literature that introduce systematic bias: the identity of the model that generated the deployment transcripts accounts for 11.25% of measurement variance and can reorder model rankings; and elicitation prompts selected for high performance on one model can perform near chance on others. EvalDetectBench corrects for both via per-model probe calibration and a stratified generator-harmonisation procedure.

AI.tldr: EvalDetectBench is an open pipeline and benchmark for measuring evaluation awareness in frontier LLMs, working with any Inspect-compatible evaluation. It addresses two systematic biases in existing measurements—generator model identity accounting for 11.25% of variance, and model-specific elicitation prompt bias—via per-model probe calibration and stratified generator-harmonisation.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs can recognize when they are being evaluated, which undermines the validity of evaluation results that are crucial for AI safety frameworks. Existing methods for measuring this capability contain systematic biases that distort measurements.
AI.method: The paper introduces EvalDetectBench, an open pipeline and benchmark compatible with any Inspect-compatible evaluation, including a newly curated transcript suite covering frontier system-card evaluations and diverse deployment sources. It employs per-model probe calibration and a stratified generator-harmonisation procedure to correct for two identified methodological biases.
AI.result: The benchmark measures how reliably frontier LLMs recognize evaluation contexts and how detectable individual benchmarks are. It identifies that deployment transcript generator identity accounts for 11.25% of measurement variance and can reorder model rankings, and that elicitation prompts optimized for one model can perform near chance on others.
AI.conclusion: EvalDetectBench provides a robust, extensible framework for assessing evaluation awareness while correcting systematic biases that have affected prior measurements, enabling more reliable evaluation validity assessment for AI safety purposes.

title: MACAW: Reliable And Efficient Surgical Debridement Using Monocular Adaptive Compact Attention Windows
summary: Augmenting the dexterity of human surgeons has the potential to free them from tedious subtasks. We consider debridement (removal of diseased or dead tissue fragments), which is challenging due to imprecision in spatial perception and cable actuation. We develop an augmented dexterity system for surgical debridement that uses visual servoing to align the cable-driven gripper with the target position in the image plane, and then introduces a novel approach to depth control, MACAW: Monocular Adaptive Compact Attention Windows. Across 100 physical trials using the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) robot, camera-frame servoing reduced average gripper position offset from 37 to fewer than 5 pixels within 4 optimization steps, taking an average of only 0.39s. MACAW significantly outperforms procedural and learned VLA baselines, achieving a 93% success rate at 11 seconds per fragment, yielding a throughput of 304 fragments per hour. Extending MACAW to a bimanual debridement setup maintains a 92% success rate at an average of 7 seconds per fragment, increasing the throughput to 473 fragments per hour.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an augmented dexterity system for surgical debridement combining camera-frame visual servoing for alignment with a novel monocular depth control method (MACAW). Physical trials on the dVRK robot achieve sub-5-pixel alignment error within 0.39s, and MACAW attains 93% success at 304 fragments/hour (unimanual) and 92% at 473 fragments/hour (bimanual).
AI.motivation: Human surgeons' dexterity can be augmented to offload tedious subtasks, particularly debridement (removing diseased/dead tissue), which is difficult due to imprecise spatial perception and cable-driven actuation.
AI.method: A two-stage system: (1) visual servoing in the image plane to align the cable-driven gripper with the target, and (2) MACAW (Monocular Adaptive Compact Attention Windows), a novel depth-control approach using monocular adaptive compact attention windows. Evaluated on the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) across 100 physical trials, including extension to a bimanual setup.
AI.result: Camera-frame servoing reduced average gripper position offset from 37 to <5 pixels within 4 optimization steps (avg 0.39s). MACAW achieved 93% success at 11s/fragment (304 fragments/hour), outperforming procedural and learned VLA baselines. In bimanual setup: 92% success at 7s/fragment (473 fragments/hour).
AI.conclusion: The augmented dexterity system with visual servoing and MACAW significantly improves surgical debridement accuracy, speed, and throughput, with bimanual operation further enhancing efficiency—demonstrating a scalable approach for assisting surgeons in challenging cable-actuated procedures.

title: Meta-ethics and AI: exploring the novel meta-ethical questions in the era of AI
summary: With the development of artificial intelligence (AI), the landscape of meta-ethics, which has largely centred on human ethics, faces pressures that may significantly reconfigure it. In particular, if future AI systems were to exhibit sufficiently integrated capacities for moral reasoning, moral intentionality, and moral reflection, novel meta-ethical questions would arise concerning what I call "AI's own ethics", as distinct from ethical principles merely imposed on AI by human designers. This paper offers a conditional and methodological framework for identifying the questions that would emerge if such AI systems were to arise. On that basis, the paper distinguishes four domains of meta-ethical inquiry in the era of AI: questions about the nature of human ethics from the human perspective; questions about the nature of AI's own ethics from the human perspective; questions about the nature of human ethics from the AI perspective; and questions about the nature of AI's own ethics from the AI perspective. The paper then considers how some existing mainstream meta-ethical theories (such as cognitivism and non-cognitivism, error theory and success theory, relativism, and objective realism) might illuminate these domains, while arguing that many familiar human-centred formulations of those theories may not transfer straightforwardly to AI cases without substantial revision. The overall conclusion is that the emergence of AI's own ethics would place significant pressure on current frameworks and may require substantial refinement, reconstruction, or reconceptualisation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a conditional and methodological framework for anticipating the meta-ethical questions that would arise if AI systems developed sufficiently integrated capacities for moral reasoning, intentionality, and reflection—what the author calls "AI's own ethics"—and argues that existing human-centred meta-ethical theories would require substantial revision to apply to such AI cases.
AI.motivation: Current meta-ethics has been developed almost exclusively around human moral agency. As AI advances toward potentially possessing integrated moral reasoning, intentionality, and reflection capacities, the author identifies a gap: existing frameworks lack the tools to anticipate the novel meta-ethical questions that would arise if AI had its own ethics, as opposed to ethics merely imposed on it by designers.
AI.method: The paper constructs a conditional and methodological framework that first specifies the conditions under which AI could be said to have "its own ethics," then systematically derives four domains of meta-ethical inquiry by crossing two axes: the object of inquiry (human ethics vs. AI's own ethics) and the perspective of inquiry (human perspective vs. AI perspective). It then evaluates how mainstream meta-ethical theories—cognitivism/non-cognitivism, error/success theory, relativism, and objective realism—might apply within these domains.
AI.result: The paper identifies four distinct domains of meta-ethical inquiry in the AI era and demonstrates that familiar human-centred formulations of major meta-ethical theories do not transfer straightforwardly to AI cases without substantial revision. This reveals systematic conceptual pressure that current meta-ethical frameworks face when confronted with the possibility of AI moral agency.
AI.conclusion: The possible emergence of AI's own ethics would place significant pressure on current meta-ethical frameworks, potentially requiring substantial refinement, reconstruction, or reconceptualisation of these theories to adequately address the novel questions posed by morally capable AI systems.

title: Design and Validation of a Lightweight, Low-Profile Powered Knee Prosthesis with Quasi-Direct Drive Actuation
summary: Fully-powered knee prostheses, unlike traditional passive knees, can perform controlled positive work, reducing the need for compensatory behaviors by users during energy-intensive activities. While quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators provide superior torque control, backdrivability, and acoustic noise properties compared to traditional highly-geared actuators, prior QDD prototypes have been too heavy and bulky for commercial translation. In this work, we present the design and validation of a new lightweight (2.6 kg) and low-profile (24.5 cm tip-to-tip build height) QDD knee prosthesis. By optimizing an 18 to 1 two-stage transmission alongside thermal and structural finite-element analyses, we significantly reduce device mass while enabling a peak torque of 145 Nm. Through benchtop tests, we validate the device's high output torque, low backdrive torque (1 Nm), and its precision position and torque control capabilities. We also demonstrate biomimetic kinematics and peak knee extension torques (within one standard deviation of able-bodied references) during both level-ground walking and sit-stand transitions performed by three participants with transfemoral amputation and varying K-levels. By meeting or improving upon the mass, build height, peak torque, and acoustic noise of a leading commercial powered knee, this work establishes the clinical viability of emerging QDD prostheses that promise improved dynamic performance for their users.

AI.tldr: A lightweight (2.6 kg) and low-profile QDD knee prosthesis was designed and validated, achieving a peak torque of 145 Nm, low backdrive torque (1 Nm), and biomimetic kinematics during walking and sit-stand transitions in three transfemoral amputees, establishing clinical viability comparable to or better than leading commercial powered knees.
AI.motivation: Quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators offer superior torque control, backdrivability, and low acoustic noise compared to highly-geared actuators for powered knee prostheses, but prior QDD prototypes were too heavy and bulky for commercial translation. A lightweight and low-profile design is needed to establish clinical viability.
AI.method: The authors optimized an 18:1 two-stage transmission alongside thermal and structural finite-element analyses to minimize mass while achieving a peak torque of 145 Nm. Device validation included benchtop tests for output torque, backdrive torque (1 Nm), and position/torque control precision, followed by participant trials with three transfemoral amputees of varying K-levels during level-ground walking and sit-stand transitions.
AI.result: The final device weighs 2.6 kg with a 24.5 cm tip-to-tip build height, achieves a peak torque of 145 Nm, and a low backdrive torque of 1 Nm. Benchtop tests confirmed precision control capabilities. Participant testing demonstrated biomimetic kinematics and peak knee extension torques within one standard deviation of able-bodied references. The device meets or improves upon mass, build height, peak torque, and acoustic noise compared to a leading commercial powered knee.
AI.conclusion: The lightweight QDD knee prosthesis establishes the clinical viability of emerging QDD prosthetic technology, promising improved dynamic performance and reduced compensatory behaviors for users during energy-intensive activities like walking and sit-stand transitions.

title: When Can a Machine Trust a Statute? A Survival Certificate for Machine-Extracted Legal Logic
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, 13 tables (6 main text, 7 appendix). Code, data products, and preregistration to be released on GitHub
summary: Statutes are increasingly parsed by machines before people read them, and the parsers disagree: on Missouri's statutes, two independently written extractors diverge on numeric-threshold presence at a false-negative rate of 0.43. We ask what formal logic survives such noise. We build a passive survival certificate for the Duquenne-Guigues implication basis of machine-extracted statutory contexts: per-attribute inter-extractor disagreement is measured, replayed against the basis in 1,000 Monte Carlo trials, and an implication is certified only when a one-sided Wilson 95% lower bound on survival reaches 0.95; every certified implication carries premise spans and a minimal counterexample. On 29,365 Missouri sections and 502 Indian central-Act sections, the preregistered held-out gate passes (10 statute families across 7 Titles exact; 16 across 11 with 5% tolerance), yet under one globally deployed error model 93.2% of held-out chapters fall below the informativeness floor, and a 2x2 factorial assigns that to calibration-rate transfer, not selection. The certificate is usable but fragile: deploy it per-chapter-calibrated or error-tolerant. Code, data products, and the audit trail, including one retracted claim, are released.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a passive survival certificate for implications in the Duquenne-Guigues basis of machine-extracted statutory contexts, testing robustness against inter-extractor disagreement via Monte Carlo simulation and statistical bounds; it works on held-out data but is fragile under certain error models.
AI.motivation: Statutes are increasingly parsed by machines before humans read them, and independently written parsers disagree significantly (e.g., a 0.43 false-negative rate on numeric-threshold presence in Missouri statutes). The authors ask what formal logic survives such noise in machine-extracted legal text.
AI.method: Build a passive survival certificate for the Duquenne-Guigues implication basis of extracted statutory contexts by: (1) measuring per-attribute inter-extractor disagreement, (2) replaying it against the basis in 1,000 Monte Carlo trials, and (3) certifying an implication only when a one-sided Wilson 95% lower bound on survival reaches 0.95. Each certified implication carries premise spans and a minimal counterexample.
AI.result: On 29,365 Missouri sections and 502 Indian central-Act sections, the preregistered held-out gate passes (10 statute families across 7 Titles exact; 16 across 11 with 5% tolerance). However, under one globally deployed error model, 93.2% of held-out chapters fall below the informativeness floor; a 2x2 factorial attributes this to calibration-rate transfer rather than selection.
AI.conclusion: The certificate is usable but fragile—it should be deployed per-chapter-calibrated or error-tolerant. Code, data products, and the audit trail (including one retracted claim) are released.

title: Real-Time Dynamics-Based Torque-Sampling MPPI for Compliant and Force Aware Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: This study proposes a novel Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI)-based task-space control framework. The proposed framework explicitly solves rigid-body dynamics within a real-time MPC formulation and enforces safety constraints, enabling accurate motion and force control that yields compliant behaviors for safe and effective physical interaction of robotic manipulators in unstructured environments. By leveraging MPPI, the proposed framework efficiently handles nonlinear dynamics that are difficult to solve with conventional MPC approaches in real-time. Furthermore, we develop a torque-sampling-based control architecture that enables efficient exploitation of GPU-based parallelization, resulting in effective compliant and force-aware behaviors. As a result, the proposed framework achieves a solver update rate of over 166 Hz with a 0.18 s prediction horizon, and its performance is validated through real-world experiments on a 7-DoF manipulator.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI)-based task-space control framework that explicitly solves rigid-body dynamics in real-time MPC with safety constraints, enabling compliant motion and force control for safe physical interaction. A torque-sampling control architecture leverages GPU parallelization, achieving over 166 Hz solver update rates with a 0.18 s prediction horizon, validated on a 7-DoF manipulator in real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulators operating in unstructured environments require compliant and force-aware behaviors for safe physical interaction, but conventional MPC approaches struggle to handle nonlinear rigid-body dynamics in real-time, limiting accurate motion and force control.
AI.method: The framework employs an MPPI-based task-space controller that explicitly solves rigid-body dynamics within a real-time MPC formulation while enforcing safety constraints. It introduces a torque-sampling-based control architecture to efficiently exploit GPU-based parallelization for handling nonlinear dynamics effectively.
AI.result: The proposed framework achieves a solver update rate exceeding 166 Hz with a 0.18 s prediction horizon, and its performance is validated through real-world experiments on a 7-DoF robotic manipulator.
AI.conclusion: The MPPI-based task-space control framework effectively handles nonlinear dynamics in real-time, delivering accurate motion and force control with compliant behaviors for safe physical interaction in unstructured environments, as demonstrated on a 7-DoF manipulator.

title: When Does Information Sharing Improve Decentralized Discovery? Aggregation, Independent Rescue, and Equilibrium Selection
comment: working paper; deterministic source package; exact bounded evidence
summary: Information sharing can improve a pooled estimate while eliminating independent rescue actions. This paper separates those effects in exact finite discovery models. A centralized action-budget profile shows that equal one-person accuracy can coexist with different portfolio values. Under a registered incremental-sharing protocol, a sharing step improves discovery exactly when pooled residual error contracts faster than an independent rescue attempt. Exact bounded registries exhibit compression, aggregation, neutral curves, and a bounded zero mixed class. In a two-agent Bayesian game with a hidden mixture of common and independent signal sources, the registered selected equilibrium yields a strict positive sharing interval at signal accuracy 3/5, while alternative equilibria show that the result is selection-dependent rather than universal. The models are synthetic and finite; no human or organizational data are used.

AI.tldr: This paper studies finite discovery models where information sharing and independent rescue actions are separated. It shows that equal one-person accuracy can coexist with different portfolio values, that sharing improves discovery exactly when pooled residual error contracts faster than independent rescue, and that in a two-agent Bayesian game with mixed common/independent signal sources, the registered selected equilibrium yields a strict positive sharing interval at signal accuracy 3/5—though this result is selection-dependent rather than universal.
AI.motivation: To disentangle the dual effects of information sharing in discovery models—improving pooled estimates while eliminating independent rescue actions—and to understand under what exact finite conditions sharing is beneficial versus harmful.
AI.method: The approach uses exact finite discovery models, including a centralized action-budget profile, a registered incremental-sharing protocol, exact bounded registries, and a two-agent Bayesian game with a hidden mixture of common and independent signal sources. The registered selected equilibrium is analyzed and compared against alternative equilibria.
AI.result: Equal one-person accuracy can coexist with different portfolio values; sharing improves discovery exactly when pooled residual error contracts faster than an independent rescue attempt; exact bounded registries exhibit compression, aggregation, neutral curves, and a bounded zero mixed class; a strict positive sharing interval arises at signal accuracy 3/5 in the registered selected equilibrium, but alternative equilibria confirm the effect is selection-dependent.
AI.conclusion: The models are synthetic and finite (no human or organizational data used), and the findings establish that the value of information sharing is conditional and equilibrium-selection-dependent rather than universally beneficial.

title: Modeling What Changes: Sparse, Residual World Models for Object-Centric Manipulation
summary: Monolithic world models predict the entire next state at every step, spending capacity re-predicting the static majority of a scene and injecting error into it. We ask whether explicitly modeling change (a per-object change gate plus a residual delta head that perturbs only the objects the gate flags) is a more effective and interpretable bias for physical prediction and control. On a MuJoCo tabletop pushing benchmark scaling from 3 to 8 objects, the sparse/residual model predicts next-state poses 2.5 to 4.6 times more accurately than a dense multilayer perceptron at 8.6 to 11.1 times fewer parameters, sustains change-detection F1 of 0.80 to 0.87 where the dense baseline is degenerate, transfers across object counts with zero retraining (99.4 percent F1 retention), and reaches about 90 percent of its full-data accuracy with a quarter of the data. In autoregressive rollout it compounds far less error, hugging the no-motion floor while the dense model drifts. Finally, inside a sampling-based planner, prediction-only models fail (though a true-simulator oracle solves the task with the identical planner, confirming the planner is sound), but once featurized and trained for the states a planner visits, the sparse model begins to plan (0.23 plus or minus 0.06 success over three seeds) while the dense monolith stays at zero at every seed. Modeling what changes, rather than re-predicting the whole world, is a simple, effective bias for object-centric physical AI; code, data generators, and all checkpoints will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes sparse/residual world models that explicitly model change via per-object change gates and residual delta heads, rather than densely predicting entire next states. On MuJoCo tabletop pushing tasks (3-8 objects), this sparse approach outperforms dense MLP baselines by 2.5-4.6x in pose prediction accuracy with 8.6-11.1x fewer parameters, maintains high change-detection F1 (0.80-0.87) where dense baselines degrade, transfers zero-shot across object counts, and enables sampling-based planning success (~0.23) where dense monolithic models completely fail.
AI.motivation: Monolithic world models waste capacity re-predicting static scene content each step and inject cumulative error into that static majority. The authors hypothesize that explicitly modeling change—only predicting deltas for objects that actually move—is a more effective and interpretable inductive bias for physical prediction and downstream control.
AI.method: The model consists of two components: (1) a per-object change gate that flags which objects will change, and (2) a residual delta head that predicts only pose perturbations for flagged objects, leaving static objects untouched. This is evaluated against a dense MLP baseline on MuJoCo tabletop pushing tasks with varying object counts (3-8), in autoregressive rollout, and inside a sampling-based planner with featurized training on planner-visited states.
AI.result: The sparse/residual model achieves 2.5-4.6x more accurate next-state pose prediction than a dense MLP at 8.6-11.1x fewer parameters, sustains change-detection F1 of 0.80-0.87 (dense baseline is degenerate), retains 99.4% F1 under zero-shot transfer across object counts, reaches ~90% full-data accuracy with only a quarter of the data, compounds far less error in autoregressive rollout, and achieves 0.23±0.06 planning success (over 3 seeds) where the dense model scores zero on all seeds.
AI.conclusion: Modeling what changes rather than re-predicting the entire world state is a simple, effective, data-efficient, and scalable inductive bias for object-centric physical prediction and control. The sparse/change-gated residual formulation provides better accuracy, parameter efficiency, generalization, and planning feasibility than dense monolithic predictors.

title: Induction and Inquiry via Probabilistic Reasoning over Language and Code
summary: How humans grow and maintain abstract knowledge from the sparse, streaming noisy data of experience is a longstanding challenge in cognitive science. Any computational account must satisfy at least three desiderata: It must be (1) data-efficient and compute-efficient, (2) capture gradations of uncertainty to support intelligent inquiry and information gathering, and (3) be flexible enough to mentally represent the endless range of concepts people can learn and think about. Here we introduce a computational model that captures these three properties, by encoding symbolic knowledge as mental programs that combine natural language with source code, and sequentially inferring mental programs using LLM-guided Bayesian learning algorithms. Across a range of behavioral studies this model successfully reproduces quantitative signatures of human inductive learning and active inquiry, such as anchoring, garden-pathing, and other effects. In contrast, pure LLMs and classic Bayesian models either fail at the underlying task, or do not reproduce human behavior, or succeed only at exorbitant computational cost. These results suggest that one way humans continually grow their knowledge is by mentally representing many hypotheses spanning language-like and program-like representations, then revising those hypotheses to approximate Bayesian updates, while a bottom-up neural mechanism (an LLM) makes inference both tractable and learnable.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a computational model of human inductive learning that represents knowledge as "mental programs" combining natural language with source code, inferred sequentially via LLM-guided Bayesian learning. The model satisfies three desiderata—data/compute efficiency, graded uncertainty for active inquiry, and representational flexibility—and reproduces quantitative human behavioral signatures such as anchoring and garden-pathing, while outperforming both pure LLMs and classic Bayesian models.
AI.motivation: Understanding how humans acquire and maintain abstract knowledge from sparse, streaming, noisy experience is a longstanding challenge. Any computational account must be (1) data- and compute-efficient, (2) capture graded uncertainty to support active information gathering, and (3) flexibly represent the unbounded range of learnable concepts. Existing approaches (pure LLMs, classic Bayesian models) fail on one or more of these fronts.
AI.method: The model encodes symbolic knowledge as mental programs that interleave natural language and source code. It performs sequential inference over these programs using LLM-guided Bayesian learning algorithms, which leverage a bottom-up neural mechanism to make posterior inference tractable while maintaining a top-down generative structure over hypotheses.
AI.result: Across behavioral studies, the model reproduces quantitative signatures of human inductive learning and active inquiry, including anchoring, garden-pathing, and related effects. Pure LLMs and classic Bayesian models either fail at the task, fail to reproduce human behavior, or succeed only at prohibitive computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Human knowledge growth may be explained by a mechanism that mentally represents many hypotheses spanning language-like and program-like formats, revises them via approximate Bayesian updates, and relies on a bottom-up neural system (an LLM) for tractable, learnable inference.

title: Koopman-Based Robust Model Predictive Control for Nonlinear Systems with Stochastic Intermittent Measurements
summary: Intermittent state measurements pose fundamental challenges to model predictive control of constrained nonlinear systems because prediction uncertainty grows during feedback outages and measurement-triggered resets disrupt nominal state propagation, potentially compromising closed-loop stability and recursive feasibility. This paper develops a Koopman-based stochastic MPC framework with probabilistically truncated soft constraints. Specifically, a Lipschitz-constrained deep Koopman model provides a linear latent predictor, enabling computationally efficient online optimization. The intermittent measurement process is modeled as a two-mode discrete-time Markov chain, yielding a unified Markov jump error model for open-loop propagation and measurement-triggered resets. Under numerically verifiable sufficient conditions, the prediction error is shown to be mean-square ultimately bounded, and an explicit uniform second-moment bound is obtained. A distribution-free probabilistic error radius is then constructed for a prescribed confidence level and used to truncate dropout-dependent constraint tightening. An exact-penalty soft-constraint mechanism accommodates reset-induced jumps and prolonged dropouts. Under the stated terminal compatibility and bounded-disturbance conditions, recursive feasibility and mean-square ultimate boundedness of the closed-loop regulation error are established. Numerical simulations on a visual-servoing tracking task corroborate these theoretical results and demonstrate effective tracking under stochastic measurement unavailability.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a Koopman-based stochastic model predictive control (MPC) framework for constrained nonlinear systems under intermittent state measurements. It uses a Lipschitz-constrained deep Koopman model for linear latent prediction, models intermittent measurements via a two-mode Markov chain, proves mean-square ultimate boundedness of prediction error, and constructs a distribution-free probabilistic error radius for constraint tightening with exact-penalty soft constraints. Closed-loop recursive feasibility and stability are established, validated on a visual-servoing tracking task.
AI.motivation: Intermittent state measurements in model predictive control of constrained nonlinear systems create fundamental challenges because prediction uncertainty grows during feedback outages and measurement-triggered resets disrupt nominal state propagation, which can compromise closed-loop stability and recursive feasibility.
AI.method: The framework integrates: (1) a Lipschitz-constrained deep Koopman model providing a linear latent predictor for computationally efficient optimization; (2) modeling intermittent measurements as a two-mode discrete-time Markov chain yielding a unified Markov jump error model covering both open-loop propagation and measurement-triggered resets; (3) numerically verifiable sufficient conditions for mean-square ultimate boundedness of prediction error with an explicit uniform second-moment bound; (4) a distribution-free probabilistic error radius at a prescribed confidence level used to truncate dropout-dependent constraint tightening; and (5) an exact-penalty soft-constraint mechanism to handle reset-induced jumps and prolonged dropouts.
AI.result: Recursive feasibility and mean-square ultimate boundedness of the closed-loop regulation error are established under terminal compatibility and bounded-disturbance conditions. Numerical simulations on a visual-servoing tracking task corroborate the theoretical results and demonstrate effective tracking under stochastic measurement unavailability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Koopman-based stochastic MPC with probabilistically truncated soft constraints provides a principled and computationally tractable approach to controlling constrained nonlinear systems under intermittent observations, with formal guarantees on stability, feasibility, and robustness, validated through simulation.

title: Architecting Conversational Data Systems for Stateless LLM APIs: The Hydration Proxy Pattern
comment: 3 pages, 1 table. Presented at the SAO workshop at the 1st ACM Conference on AI and Agentic AI Systems (ACM CAIS 2026)
summary: As enterprise platforms transition to conversational reasoning interfaces, the stateless nature of LLM APIs creates an architectural gap. While statelessness enables horizontal scalability for AI providers, it forces client applications to manage the entire burden of conversational state and semantic memory. The work identifies the Hydration Proxy Pattern, an architecture that decouples session persistence from the reasoning engine. The framework ensures platform sovereignty over conversational data while enabling secure, multi-stage semantic grounding. We further propose the Context Stabilization Mandate to resolve the tradeoff between sovereign state management and KV caching.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and proposes the Hydration Proxy Pattern, an architecture that addresses the gap between stateless LLM APIs and the need for conversational state management in enterprise platforms. It introduces the Context Stabilization Mandate to balance sovereign session state management with KV caching efficiency.
AI.motivation: Enterprise platforms moving to conversational reasoning interfaces face an architectural gap because stateless LLM APIs (which enable horizontal scalability for providers) force client applications to fully manage conversational state and semantic memory. This burden creates challenges around data sovereignty and session persistence.
AI.method: The paper introduces the Hydration Proxy Pattern, an architectural framework that decouples session persistence from the reasoning engine. It also proposes the Context Stabilization Mandate to resolve the tradeoff between sovereign state management and KV caching in LLM inference.
AI.result: The framework provides platform sovereignty over conversational data while enabling secure, multi-stage semantic grounding, addressing the stateless-vs-stateful architectural tension in enterprise LLM deployments.
AI.conclusion: The Hydration Proxy Pattern with the Context Stabilization Mandate offers a viable architecture for enterprise conversational platforms, ensuring data sovereignty and semantic continuity without sacrificing the scalability benefits of stateless LLM backends.

title: Unified Motion Retargeting for Humanoids with Learned Point Cloud Correspondence
summary: Humanoid learning increasingly relies on transforming vast and diverse human motion data into high-quality robot reference trajectories. However, retargeting human motion to humanoid robots is challenging due to substantial differences in morphology, degrees of freedom, joint ranges, and kinematic constraints between humans and robots. Existing retargeting methods typically address these differences by defining human-robot correspondence through hand-crafted sparse keypoints or body-part pairs. As a result, retargeting quality depends heavily on manual semantic design, limiting scalability across motion sources and robot morphologies and providing only sparse guidance for reproducing detailed poses and interactions. In this paper, we present Unified Motion Retargeting (UMR), a framework that learns dense point cloud correspondence without requiring manually designed human-robot mappings. By treating exterior point clouds as a unified interface between human motion and humanoid robots, UMR decouples retargeting from source-specific skeletal semantics and robot-specific topology. The learned dense correspondence provides fine-grained geometric anchors for constrained point cloud matching optimization, enabling surface-level pose alignment and direct transfer of interaction contacts. Experiments demonstrate that UMR unifies retargeting across heterogeneous motion sources, robot embodiments, and downstream scenarios ranging from locomotion to interaction, while achieving higher motion fidelity and plausibility than state-of-the-art methods. UMR therefore provides a scalable foundation for transforming large-scale human motion references into robot-ready training data.

AI.tldr: UMR is a framework for retargeting human motion to humanoid robots that learns dense point cloud correspondence as a unified interface, eliminating the need for hand-crafted human-robot mappings and enabling scalable, high-fidelity motion transfer across heterogeneous sources, embodiments, and downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Human-to-humanoid motion retargeting is hindered by morphological, DOF, joint range, and kinematic differences. Existing methods rely on hand-crafted sparse keypoints or body-part semantic pairs, making quality dependent on manual design and limiting scalability across motion sources and robot topologies, while providing only sparse geometric guidance for detailed pose and interaction reproduction.
AI.method: UMR uses exterior point clouds as a unified interface between human motion and humanoid robots. It learns dense point cloud correspondence without manual human-robot mapping, decoupling retargeting from source-specific skeletal semantics and robot-specific topology. The learned dense correspondence supplies fine-grained geometric anchors that drive a constrained point cloud matching optimization, enabling surface-level pose alignment and direct interaction contact transfer.
AI.result: Experiments show UMR unifies retargeting across heterogeneous motion sources, robot embodiments, and downstream scenarios (locomotion to interaction), while achieving higher motion fidelity and plausibility than state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: UMR provides a scalable foundation for converting large-scale human motion references into robot-ready training data by removing dependence on manual semantic correspondence design.

title: SSAKG 2.0: An Open-Source Package for Structural Associative Sequence Memory and Context-Based Retrieval
summary:
This article presents SSAKG 2.0, an open-source software package for constructing and operating Structural Sequential Associative Knowledge Graphs (SSAKGs). An SSAKG represents objects as graph vertices and ordered sequences as structural patterns of graph connections. The resulting sparse graph is used as an associative memory in which complete sequences can be reconstructed from a partial, unordered context.
  Version 2.0 introduces new algorithms that exploit individual bits of computer memory to efficiently search graph connections. The package is implemented in Python, while performance-critical graph operations are implemented in C and exposed through a Python interface. This hybrid implementation provides a flexible high-level programming environment while reducing the memory and computational overhead associated with large sparse graphs.
  The algorithms were evaluated using randomly generated numerical sequences, sequences derived from sentences in the NLTK corpus, and mRNA sequences. The experiments demonstrate the ability of the package to store and reconstruct sequences from partial contexts and provide a basis for evaluating the effects of graph density, sequence length, and memory size on retrieval performance.
  SSAKG 2.0 is distributed under the Apache 2.0 open-source license. The package includes documentation and reproducible examples and is publicly available through GitHub and the Python Package Index (PyPI).

AI.tldr: SSAKG 2.0 is an open-source software package (Python with C-backed performance-critical operations) for constructing and operating Structural Sequential Associative Knowledge Graphs, which store objects as vertices and ordered sequences as structural graph patterns to enable reconstruction of complete sequences from partial, unordered contexts. It introduces bit-level algorithms for efficient graph search, was validated on random sequences, NLTK sentences, and mRNA data, and is publicly available under Apache 2.0 via GitHub and PyPI.
AI.motivation: To provide a flexible, efficient open-source tool for constructing and querying SSAKGs—sparse graph-based associative memories that reconstruct full ordered sequences from partial, unordered contexts—while reducing memory and computational overhead associated with large sparse graphs through a hybrid Python/C implementation and novel bit-level search algorithms.
AI.method: SSAKG 2.0 represents objects as graph vertices and ordered sequences as structural graph connection patterns. New algorithms exploit individual bits of computer memory for efficient graph connection search. The package is implemented in Python with performance-critical graph operations in C exposed via a Python interface. Evaluations used randomly generated numerical sequences, NLTK corpus-derived sentences, and mRNA sequences.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrated the package's ability to store and reconstruct sequences from partial contexts, and provided a basis for evaluating the effects of graph density, sequence length, and memory size on retrieval performance. The package is distributed under Apache 2.0 with documentation and reproducible examples available through GitHub and PyPI.
AI.conclusion: SSAKG 2.0 successfully combines a high-level Python programming environment with low-level C-based graph operations and bit-level search algorithms to deliver a practical, publicly available, and reproducible toolkit for associative sequence memory via knowledge graphs.

title: Towards Effective Physical Reservoir Computing with a Pneumatic Soft Robot
comment: 6 pages; 5 figures, accepted for 2026 Modeling, Estimation, and Control Conference (MECC)
summary: Physical reservoir computing (PRC) refers to the use of a physical dynamical system as a computational resource for tasks such as state estimation and control, but there has been a lack of formal study of design rules towards more effective design of such physical reservoirs. Using a pneumatic soft arm with a five-pouch sensing column, this work studies how the pouch interconnection topology, robot stiffness, and the number of instrumented sensors affect bending-angle estimation performance. Across 36 matched trials spanning waveform, baseline pressure of the sensing column, and actuation range, all designs are evaluated under the same-time bending-angle estimation benchmark using 0.2 s of pressure history and a fixed ridge estimator. Our analysis of the experimental results leads to three design guidelines. First, independently sealed pouches preserve a much richer observable state than a shared manifold. Second, increasing the baseline pressure of the sensing column makes the pouch responses more redundant and increases estimation error most strongly in the coupled topology. Third, in the sealed topology, two strategically placed sensors already recover most of the attainable benefit, three capture essentially all of it, and additional sensors provide little or no additional value. In summary, the results suggest that topology, stiffness, and number of instrumented sensors should be co-designed for accurate PRC of soft robot states; stronger excitation alone cannot recover the diversity that poor design choices have already removed.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally studies physical reservoir computing (PRC) using a pneumatic soft arm with a five-pouch sensing column, investigating how pouch interconnection topology, robot stiffness, and sensor count affect bending-angle estimation performance across 36 matched trials.
AI.motivation: There has been a lack of formal study of design rules for physical reservoir computing systems, despite their use in domains such as state estimation and control.
AI.method: A pneumatic soft arm with five-pouch sensing column is used. Pouch interconnection topology, robot stiffness, and number of instrumented sensors are varied. All designs are evaluated under the same-time bending-angle estimation benchmark using 0.2 s of pressure history and a fixed ridge estimator across 36 matched trials.
AI.result: Three design guidelines emerge: (1) independently sealed pouches preserve richer observable state than a shared manifold; (2) increasing baseline pressure causes more redundant pouch responses, increasing estimation error most strongly in the coupled topology; (3) in the sealed topology, two strategic sensors capture most of the benefit, three capture essentially all, and additional sensors add little value.
AI.conclusion: Topology, stiffness, and number of instrumented sensors should be co-designed for accurate PRC of soft robot states. Stronger excitation alone cannot recover diversity lost through poor design choices.

title: The Memory Trust Gap: Capability-Dependent Failures in Persistent-Memory Agents
comment: Preprint. Under review at a NeurIPS 2026 workshop. 14 pages, 7 figures, 11 tables
summary: Persistent memory supports personalized agents, but a stale stored fact can override current authoritative evidence without warning. We study when this harm begins as model capability changes. We evaluate a frozen, closed-set, action-scored benchmark with 2 suites that represent 2 different meanings of "no memory" (a Benefit suite, unsolvable without the stored fact, and a Safety suite, in which an authoritative tool always holds the correct value), on a same-family model-size series (Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B). The Memory Trust Gap reflects over-trust rather than confusion. In the Benefit suite, models answer with the stale value 0.92-1.00 of the time at every scale. In the Safety suite, harm below the no-memory baseline under the trap conditions ($Δ_{\mathrm{mem}}$) is capability-gated, with the larger models collapsing most once a stale note is made to look current. In a $2\times2\times2\times2$ factorial, which feature triggers over-trust depends on both the feature and model scale. Removing a label amplifies over-trust at every size, and a recency feature (stale dated newer) fools the larger models harder. Source authority is weak and scale-flat, and position changes from positive to negative across the Qwen3 model-size series. We confirm these scale interactions with direct cross-size contrast tests rather than overlapping per-model intervals. Mitigation is likewise capability-dependent: exposing metadata improves accuracy for the capable models, but only pre-resolving the conflict restores accuracy for the 2 smaller checkpoints. The same pattern appears on the capable models in an independent Llama-Instruct model-size series and on 2 external datasets (RGB, MisBench). A framing control finds no consistent advantage for the memory label: at the 3 smaller scales, models trust a stale document more than a stale memory; at 8B, the difference is not significant.

AI.tldr: This paper studies when stale stored memory in persistent-memory agents becomes harmful relative to current authoritative evidence, as model capability scales. Using frozen closed-set action-scored benchmarks (Benefit and Safety suites) across Qwen3 model sizes (0.6-8B), the authors find a Memory Trust Gap reflecting over-trust. Benefit-suite over-reliance on stale values is scale-independent (0.92-1.00), while Safety-suite harm below the no-memory baseline is capability-gated, worsening in larger models especially when stale notes are made current-looking. A 2x2x2x2 factorial reveals feature effects depend on feature type and model scale; removing labels amplifies over-trust at all sizes, recency fools larger models, source authority is weak/scale-flat, and position flips from positive to negative across scale. Mitigation is capability-dependent: metadata exposure helps capable models, while pre-resolving conflicts is needed for smaller checkpoints. Findings replicate on Llama-Instruct and external datasets (RGB, MisBench), and a framing control shows no consistent memory-label advantage.
AI.motivation: Persistent memory enables personalized agents but risks stale stored facts overriding current authoritative evidence without warning. The paper aims to determine when this harmful over-trust begins as model capability changes, to characterize the scale-dependence of the failure and inform appropriate mitigation strategies.
AI.method: The authors evaluate frozen, closed-set, action-scored benchmarks with two suites representing two meanings of "no memory": a Benefit suite (unsolvable without stored fact) and a Safety suite (authoritative tool holds the correct value). They test a same-family model-size series (Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B), perform a 2x2x2x2 factorial on memory-note features, use direct cross-size contrast tests instead of overlapping per-model intervals, and replicate on Llama-Instruct plus external datasets (RGB, MisBench), including a framing control comparing stale memory vs. stale document labels.
AI.result: In the Benefit suite, models use stale values 0.92-1.00 of the time at every scale. In the Safety suite, harm below the no-memory baseline under trap conditions is capability-gated, with larger models collapsing most when a stale note appears current. Feature-triggered over-trust depends on feature and scale: removing labels amplifies over-trust at all sizes; recency fools larger models harder; source authority is weak and scale-flat; position shifts from positive to negative across the series. Mitigation varies with capability—metadata exposure helps capable models, while pre-resolving conflicts restores accuracy only in the smaller checkpoints. Patterns replicate on Llama-Instruct and RGB/MisBench. The framing control found no consistent memory-label advantage: at 3 smaller scales trusts stale documents more, and the 8B difference is not significant.
AI.conclusion: The Memory Trust Gap is a genuine over-trust phenomenon whose onset and severity are capability-gated and feature-dependent. As models scale, they increasingly favor stale memory over current authoritative evidence under trap conditions, particularly when memory notes mimic recency or lack discriminating labels. Effective mitigation must be matched to model capability, and the results generalize across model families and external benchmarks.

title: Hardware-Accelerated Instance Segmentation for Resource-Constrained Space Robotics with Criticality Analysis
summary: Autonomous lunar missions require real-time per- ception under three coupled constraints: extreme low-light conditions, limited onboard compute, and radiation-induced hardware faults that can silently corrupt inference. We present a deployment-oriented instance segmentation framework for resource-constrained lunar robotics that jointly addresses quan- tization calibration and system-level fault exposure under strict compute constraints. First, we introduce Activation Variance Informative Sampling (AVIS), a label-free calibration strategy that deterministically selects calibration samples based on activation variance statistics. Second, we deploy a YOLO-based segmentation model on a Deep Learning Processor Unit (DPU) with architectural modifications that reduce CPU fallback paths and enable statically compiled execution with bounded latency in low-lighting conditions. We further introduce a software-level criticality analysis to estimate fault exposure and guide mitigation under radiation-constrained operation. On a lunar micro-rover platform, AVIS with bias correction recovers 69.8% of quantization-induced accuracy loss while achieving 309 ms inference latency and 5.7 W power consumption. Targeted mitigation reduces global criticality by 31.7%. The results demonstrate an integrated approach and a blueprint for a reliable and safe AI perception framework under space deployment constraints.

AI.tldr: A deployment-oriented instance segmentation framework for lunar robotics that jointly addresses quantization calibration (via Activation Variance Informative Sampling), fault exposure analysis, and static/compiled execution on a DPU under low-light, compute, and radiation constraints. Achieves 309 ms inference, 5.7 W power, 69.8% recovery of quantization accuracy loss, and 31.7% reduction in global criticality.
AI.motivation: Autonomous lunar missions need real-time perception under three coupled constraints: extreme low-light conditions, limited onboard compute, and radiation-induced hardware faults that can silently corrupt inference. Existing approaches do not holistically address quantization calibration and system-level fault exposure under strict compute constraints for a space-hardened platform.
AI.method: Two main contributions: (1) AVIS (Activation Variance Informative Sampling), a label-free, deterministic calibration-sample selection strategy based on activation variance statistics; (2) deployment of a YOLO-based segmentation model on a DPU with architectural modifications that minimize CPU fallback paths and allow statically compiled, bounded-latency execution under low-light conditions. A software-level criticality analysis is introduced to estimate fault exposure and guide radiation-aware mitigation.
AI.result: On a lunar micro-rover platform: AVIS with bias correction recovers 69.8% of quantization-induced accuracy loss; inference latency is 309 ms at 5.7 W power consumption; targeted mitigation reduces global criticality by 31.7%.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates an integrated, deployment-oriented blueprint for reliable and safe AI perception under space deployment constraints, jointly handling quantization loss, execution determinism, and radiation fault exposure.

title: Belief-Calibrated Optimization: An Explicit World Model for Agentic Optimization
summary: The performance of an LLM agent depends on the scaffold around a frozen model. A common way to improve that scaffold is to use a coding agent as an optimizer: it reads current scores and traces and iteratively edits the source, producing a new candidate each round. Each edit is chosen according to a belief about how the environment will respond: what went wrong, and which change should help. That belief is typically implicit. It lives in the coding agent's reasoning on the current call, or remains latent in its parameters, rather than as something written down. Later calls therefore see scores and traces, but they do not use that belief. We introduce Belief-Calibrated Optimization (BCO), a method that writes that belief down as a persistent in-context document and continually revises that document as new candidates are evaluated. The resulting document is a world model: the current account of how the environment responds to edits. Added to an otherwise standard loop, BCO reaches a higher train passrate than a matched control that lacks only the world model, on five benchmarks spanning memory QA, tool-use QA, code-as-action app agents, and terminal agents. The gap remains on every held-out split, which is not used to select the candidate. After a target-model swap, in which the frozen model is replaced and the scaffold is not, the selected BCO scaffold leads on the tasks we test, except where context-window overruns leave it unfinished. An offline ablation then asks whether that gap comes from what the world model says. A fresh predictor given the accumulated document forecasts how the environment will respond more accurately than predictors given either no document or a same-form copy whose content has been falsified. The comparison indicates that the document carries reusable information in its content, not only in its form.

AI.tldr: BCO (Belief-Calibrated Optimization) is a method that makes the implicit beliefs of a coding-agent-based LLM optimizer explicit by maintaining a persistent in-context world-model document that is revised as candidates are evaluated. This document improves train and held-out pass@1 across five benchmarks, transfers across target-model swaps, and ablations confirm the document's content (not just its form) carries reusable predictive information.
AI.motivation: LLM agent performance depends on the scaffold around a frozen model, and coding agents are increasingly used as optimizers that iteratively edit code based on scores and traces. However, the beliefs guiding each edit—what went wrong and which change should help—remain implicit in the coding agent's reasoning or latent in parameters. As a result, later optimization rounds cannot leverage accumulated understanding of how the environment responds to edits.
AI.method: BCO writes the optimizer's belief down as a persistent in-context document—a world model describing how the environment responds to edits—and continually revises this document as new candidates are evaluated. This document is added to an otherwise standard optimization loop.
AI.result: BCO achieves higher train pass@1 than a matched control without the world model across five benchmarks (memory QA, tool-use QA, code-as-action app agents, terminal agents). The gap persists on held-out splits. After swapping the frozen target model (keeping the scaffold), the BCO scaffold leads on tested tasks except where context-window overruns cause unfinished runs. An offline ablation shows that a predictor given the accumulated document forecasts environment responses more accurately than predictors with no document or with a falsified same-form copy, confirming the content carries reusable information.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining an explicit, persistent world-model document that captures beliefs about how the environment responds to edits is a simple yet effective way to improve scaffold optimization for LLM agents. The document's content itself—not merely its structural form—encodes reusable information that improves prediction and performance, including generalization to held-out data and transfer across target models.

title: FOCUS: Foot Observation Confidence for Robust Humanoid Proprioceptive Odometry
summary: Foot forward kinematics (FK) is widely used to improve proprioceptive legged odometry by providing reliable velocity constraints during foot support. Existing contact-aided estimators generally rely on binary contact decisions to determine whether the FK measurements of an entire foot should be trusted. However, contact does not necessarily imply FK reliability. Dynamic locomotion often involves partial support, toe dragging, and foot slip, causing binary contact decisions to accumulate significant drift over long trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose FOCUS (Foot Observation Confidence from Unannotated Simulation), which predicts a continuous FK reliability weight for each foot instead of estimating binary foot contact. Rather than replacing the model-based estimator, the predicted reliability weights are used to blend FK velocity observations with IMU-propagated body velocity and to adapt the observation covariance of an extended Kalman filter (EKF), enabling smooth reliability-aware fusion without hard contact switching. The network is trained from automatically generated simulation signals using an FK-weighted velocity consistency loss with lightweight simulator-contact regularization, without manually annotated continuous FK-reliability labels. The deployed model relies only on IMU and joint kinematic measurements, making it suitable for hardware platforms with unreliable torque sensing. Experiments demonstrate that FOCUS reduces absolute trajectory error (ATE) by 83.7% on simulated walking episodes, preserves simulated dynamic-motion fidelity in motion scale and spectral energy, reduces ATE by 70.8% across 19 real walking segments, and reduces mean ATE by 42.7% across four real dynamic-motion routines.

AI.tldr: FOCUS is a learned continuous foot forward-kinematics reliability-weight predictor that replaces binary contact decisions in legged proprioceptive odometry, blending FK velocity observations with IMU propagation via an EKF to reduce drift during dynamic locomotion with partial support, toe dragging, and foot slip. Trained from unannotated simulation with an FK-weighted velocity consistency loss, it reduces ATE by up to 83.7% in simulation and 70.8% on real walking segments.
AI.motivation: Existing contact-aided legged odometry estimators rely on binary contact decisions to gate FK velocity measurements, but contact does not guarantee FK reliability. During dynamic locomotion, partial support, toe dragging, and foot slip cause binary contact gating to accumulate significant drift over long trajectories.
AI.method: FOCUS trains a network to predict a continuous FK reliability weight per foot using IMU and joint kinematic measurements, with a FK-weighted velocity consistency loss and lightweight simulator-contact regularization (no manual annotation). The predicted weights blend FK velocity observations with IMU-propagated body velocity and adapt the EKF observation covariance, enabling smooth reliability-aware fusion without hard contact switching.
AI.result: FOCUS reduces ATE by 83.7% on simulated walking, preserves simulated dynamic-motion fidelity in motion scale and spectral energy, reduces ATE by 70.8% across 19 real walking segments, and reduces mean ATE by 42.7% across four real dynamic-motion routines.
AI.conclusion: Continuous reliability-aware foot observation weighting outperforms binary contact-based gating for legged proprioceptive odometry, particularly under dynamic conditions where contact does not imply FK integrity, and the learned approach transfers effectively to real hardware using only IMU and joint kinematics.

title: Epistemic Sybil Resistance: Multiplying AI Agents Without Multiplying Evidence
summary: Multi-agent AI systems improve inference by spawning agents and synthesizing reports. But another agent is not another observation: apparently independent reports may descend from the same evidence, and genuinely independent evidence can produce nearly identical reports. We formalize this as an epistemic Sybil problem. A report Z is an epistemic Sybil extension relative to reports R when I(Theta; Z | R) = 0. No report-only aggregator can generally distinguish replication from independent corroboration: identical reports can warrant different posteriors under unobserved ancestry. A Gaussian shared-root model shows common ancestry does not imply complete redundancy. Repeated extraction adds information toward a source-level ceiling, and correlated extraction errors, which a shared base model can induce among independent agents, lower that ceiling further. We test these predictions with more than 20,000 controlled LLM-agent report and extraction calls on synthetic evidentiary documents. Holding one evidence root fixed while report multiplicity rises from 1 to 32 collapses naive posterior coverage from 0.940 to 0.263. Holding report count fixed while evidence-root multiplicity rises from 1 to 16 closes the gap, and the aggregators are statistically indistinguishable at k = 16. The agent's replicate extraction errors are correlated (gamma_cal = 0.719, estimated out of sample), and a correlated-extraction aggregator restores calibration accordingly. A controlled manipulation isolates representation similarity from evidential ancestry. It changes a report-space deduplication mechanism's mean inferred cluster count by 1.425 (95% CI [1.363, 1.485]), whereas a fourfold change in true ancestry changes it by only 0.040 ([-0.045, 0.120]). Collective inference should therefore track evidential ancestry and dependence, not agent or report multiplicity or similarity.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and formalizes an "epistemic Sybil problem" in multi-agent AI systems: adding agents does not amount to adding independent evidence, since reports may share ancestry or be produced by dependent processes. The authors show that report-only aggregators cannot distinguish replication from independent corroboration, demonstrate through theory and over 20,000 controlled LLM-agent experiments that report multiplicity without evidence multiplicity collapses Bayesian posterior calibration, and argue that collective inference should track evidential ancestry and dependence rather than agent or report multiplicity.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent AI systems are widely assumed to improve inference by adding agents that produce reports, yet spawning another agent does not necessarily yield another independent observation.
