A candidate is invalid if its script fails or returns a different answer, or trivial if a model answers it without the software. We present ToolGate, which treats every generated item as a proposal and keeps it only if three gates pass. First, an executable solution script must reproduce the proposed answer when run with the scientific software. Second, randomized no-tool screening rejects candidates that models can already solve from the prompt alone. Third, a tool-using agent must solve each survivor within a fixed time limit. We instantiate ToolGate in FEniCSx with 500 generation attempts. The local-verification gate retains 478 candidates. For final reporting, we rescreen this pool after generation: two randomized no-tool screens exclude 222 from the reported pool, and direct GPT-5.5 API calls at medium reasoning (the API default) exclude another 121. Of the remaining 135, a GPT-5.5 Codex CLI agent with access to FEniCSx solves 130; exact deduplication leaves 128 unique protocol survivors. ToolGate turns repeated answer checking and difficulty screening into an auditable process while leaving domain design and final review to experts.

AI.tldr: ToolGate is a three-gate verification pipeline for automatically generating benchmark items: executable-script reproduction, randomized no-tool screening to reject trivially answerable questions, and tool-using-agent time-limited solving. Applied to FEniCSx scientific computing benchmarks, 128 unique protocol-surviving items were produced from 500 generation attempts.
AI.motivation: Traditional benchmark construction by domain experts is costly in per-item labor. Language models can propose candidate questions cheaply, but the bottleneck is accepting only valid, non-trivial, and suitably difficult items.
AI.method: ToolGate treats every generated item as a proposal and keeps it only if three gates pass: (1) an executable solution script must reproduce the proposed answer when run with scientific software (local verification); (2) randomized no-tool screening rejects candidates that models can solve from the prompt alone (triviality filter); (3) a tool-using agent must solve each surviving candidate within a fixed time limit (difficulty gate). It is instantiated in FEniCSx with 500 generation attempts and final rescreening after generation.
AI.result: From 500 generation attempts, the local-verification gate retained 478 candidates. Two randomized no-tool screens excluded 222 from the reported pool, and GPT-5.5 API calls at medium reasoning excluded another 121. Of the remaining 135, a GPT-5.5 Codex CLI agent with FEniCSx access solved 130, and exact deduplication left 128 unique protocol survivors.
AI.conclusion: ToolGate transforms repeated answer checking and difficulty screening into an auditable, automated process, while preserving domain design and final expert review. It reduces human per-item labor while maintaining benchmark quality through rigorous automated filtering.

title: Advancing Accessible Underwater Robotics: The Mini-Girona I-AUV at RAMI 2025
summary: The Mini-Girona Intervention Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (I-AUV) represents an advancement in accessible underwater robotics, designed to bridge the gap between costly, specialized research AUVs and basic Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs). Developed with a focus on affordability and usability, the Mini-Girona, priced at approximately $50,000, integrates advanced components such as a 5-DOF manipulator arm, stereo vision, and AI-driven processing for autonomous navigation and intervention tasks. This paper presents the design and development of the Mini-Girona, detailing its performance during the RAMI 2025 student competition. Despite challenges such as thermal management issues and restricted team access, the Mini-Girona achieved second place overall, excelling in vision-based perception and intervention tasks. This work highlights the platform's potential as a tool for underwater robotics research and education, fostering innovation in real-world underwater applications.

AI.tldr: The Mini-Girona is a $50,000 Intervention Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (I-AUV) that bridges the gap between expensive research AUVs and basic ROVs. It integrates a 5-DOF manipulator, stereo vision, and AI processing for autonomous navigation and intervention. Despite thermal management issues and restricted team access, it placed second at the RAMI 2025 student competition, excelling in vision perception and intervention, demonstrating its value as an affordable research and education platform.
AI.motivation: To make underwater robotics research and intervention capabilities more accessible by developing an affordable I-AUV platform that fills the gap between costly specialized research AUVs and basic ROVs, thereby lowering barriers to education and research in real-world underwater applications.
AI.method: The paper presents the design and development of the Mini-Girona I-AUV, incorporating a 5-DOF manipulator arm, stereo vision, and AI-driven processing for autonomous navigation and intervention tasks, followed by empirical performance evaluation during the RAMI 2025 student competition.
AI.result: The Mini-Girona achieved second place overall at the RAMI 2025 competition, demonstrating strong performance particularly in vision-based perception and intervention tasks, despite encountering thermal management challenges and limited team access during development.
AI.conclusion: The Mini-Girona demonstrates strong potential as a cost-effective platform for underwater robotics research and education, promoting innovation in real-world underwater applications through its accessible price point and competitive intervention capabilities.

title: CHIME: Credit-Aware Hierarchical Memory Evolution for Long-Horizon Agentic Planning
summary: Planning is a central capability that enables agents to decompose complex long-horizon tasks into manageable steps. Test-time search and training-based methods improve planning but incur high inference costs or require expensive training data. Self-evolving memory instead accumulates reusable experience from agent interaction outcomes into an external memory bank, so planning capability keeps improving at inference time without parameter updates. However, existing self-evolving memory methods share an inherent credit assignment problem: they rely on final task outcomes as feedback, but such outcomes conflate plan quality with execution errors and environmental factors, so the accumulated planning experience is often biased and noisy. To address this problem, we propose Credit-Aware Hierarchical Memory Evolution (CHIME), a self-evolving memory framework that maintains a separate planning bank and execution bank and follows an attribute-before-memorize principle: CHIME first attributes each task outcome to the plan, the execution, both, or neither, and then updates only the corresponding memory bank. Extensive experiments on four long-horizon agent benchmarks show that CHIME consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-based and self-evolving memory baselines. Further analyses reveal several interesting findings. For example, CHIME accumulates effective memory with far fewer items. In addition, the learned memory values faithfully reflect downstream utility: high-quality planning memories are more valuable than execution memories. Finally, the accumulated memory effectively transfers across backbone models. Code will be released at https://github.com/ATH-MaaS/Marco-DeepResearch.

AI.tldr: CHIME is a self-evolving memory framework that addresses credit assignment in planning by maintaining separate planning and execution memory banks, attributing task outcomes before memorizing them. It consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on four long-horizon agent benchmarks, requires fewer memory items, and learns memories that transfer across backbone models.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving memory methods suffer from a credit assignment problem: they use final task outcomes as feedback, but these outcomes conflate plan quality with execution errors and environmental factors, leading to biased and noisy accumulated planning experience.
AI.method: CHIME maintains two separate memory banks (planning bank and execution bank) and follows an attribute-before-memorize principle. It first attributes each task outcome to one of four categories: plan, execution, both, or neither, and then updates only the corresponding memory bank based on this attribution.
AI.result: CHIME consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-based and self-evolving memory baselines across four long-horizon agent benchmarks. Analysis shows CHIME accumulates effective memory with far fewer items, learned memory values faithfully reflect downstream utility (high-quality planning memories are more valuable), and accumulated memory effectively transfers across backbone models.
AI.conclusion: Credit-aware hierarchical memory separation resolves the credit assignment problem in self-evolving memory, enabling more efficient and effective planning improvement at inference time without parameter updates or expensive training.

title: Latent Cluster Analysis for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models are increasingly used in robotics for their ability to ground language and perception into action, yet the internal representations driving their behaviour remain poorly understood. We propose LAVLA, a framework for latent cluster analysis of VLA models, and conduct a layer-wise study of the state-of-the-art GR00T N1.5 model, with particular focus on its action decoder. To better characterise the latent space during action diffusion, we introduce a cross-attention-based embedding-weighting method that amplifies relevant features while suppressing less informative ones. Quantitative evaluation shows that weighted clustering consistently outperforms the baseline. To improve interpretability, we extract human-interpretable concepts for each cluster, linking latent representations to semantic descriptions. Our analysis shows that latent clusters progressively disentangle spatiotemporal and kinematic features, with representations becoming more refined in the middle layers and stabilising toward the output. As such, LAVLA advances the interpretability of language-driven robotic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LAVLA, a latent cluster analysis framework for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, applied layer-wise to the GR00T N1.5 model. A cross-attention-based embedding-weighting method improves clustering, revealing that latent clusters progressively disentangle spatiotemporal and kinematic features, becoming refined in middle layers and stabilizing toward the output.
AI.motivation: VLA models are increasingly used in robotics for grounding language and perception into action, yet their internal representations remain poorly understood. The authors aim to improve interpretability of language-driven robotic systems by analyzing the latent space of VLA models.
AI.method: The framework (LAVLA) performs latent cluster analysis on VLA models, focusing on the action decoder of GR00T N1.5. A cross-attention-based embedding-weighting method is introduced to amplify relevant features and suppress less informative ones during action diffusion. Human-interpretable concepts are then extracted for each cluster to link latent representations to semantic descriptions.
AI.result: Quantitative evaluation shows weighted clustering consistently outperforms the baseline. The analysis reveals that latent clusters progressively disentangle spatiotemporal and kinematic features, with representations becoming more refined in middle layers and stabilizing toward the output.
AI.conclusion: LAVLA advances the interpretability of language-driven robotic systems by providing a systematic framework for understanding how VLA models form and organize latent representations across layers, with evidence of progressive feature disentanglement and stabilization.

title: Beyond Outcome Gaps: Process-Aware Fairness Diagnosis for LLM-based Multi-Agent Decision Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly considered for high-stakes decision-making, yet outcome-based fairness audits can miss where risks arise within the decision trajectory. We present SCOPED-Hiring, a process-aware fairness diagnosis pipeline for LLM-based hiring MAS. SCOPED-Hiring constructs controlled resume variants, runs role-based hiring committees, logs over 311K structured decision trajectories, and converts trajectory fields into quantitative fairness signals organized by six diagnostic lenses: final outcome, counterfactual, process, pathway, dynamic, and design effects. SCOPED-Hiring reveals that balanced final hire rates can mask hidden trajectory unfairness in multi-agent decision trajectories: career gaps trigger suspicion, proxy cues shape qualification judgments, and identity cues lead to unequal investigation. Targeted repair guided by these diagnoses reduces total layered burden by 72.3% while shifting the hire rate by only 1.86 pp, showing that process diagnosis can guide effective repair. Project Page: https://scoped-hiring-project-page.vercel.app/

AI.tldr: SCOPED-Hiring is a process-aware fairness diagnosis pipeline for LLM-based hiring multi-agent systems that constructs controlled resume variants, logs over 311K decision trajectories, and analyzes them through six diagnostic lenses to uncover hidden trajectory unfairness that outcome-only auditing misses, demonstrating that targeted diagnosis-guided repair reduces layered burden by 72.3% with minimal hire rate shift.
AI.motivation: Outcome-based fairness audits of LLM multi-agent systems can fail to identify where and how biases arise within decision processes, particularly in high-stakes hiring contexts where hidden trajectory-level unfairness may persist despite balanced final outcomes.
AI.method: SCOPED-Hiring builds controlled resume variants, deploys role-based hiring committee agents, logs over 311K structured decision trajectories, and transforms trajectory fields into quantitative fairness signals across six lenses: final outcome, counterfactual, process, pathway, dynamic, and design effects.
AI.result: The pipeline reveals that balanced final hire rates can mask hidden trajectory unfairness—career gaps trigger suspicion, proxy cues skew qualification judgments, and identity cues cause unequal investigation. Diagnosis-guided targeted repair cuts total layered burden by 72.3% while changing the hire rate by only 1.86 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Process-aware fairness diagnosis is essential for LLM-based MAS in high-stakes domains, as it uncovers biases invisible to outcome-level metrics and enables targeted, minimally disruptive repairs that substantially reduce composite fairness burdens.

title: HINT: Human-Intent Inception for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Humans can perform complex manipulations given a simple intent through an overall instruction, while continuously adapting to evolving visual observations. However, current vision-language action (VLA) models and other action policies struggle to realize this high-level intelligent behavior under dense, evolving visual inputs and sparse language guidance. Visual correlations can then dominate semantic intent, leading actions to follow visual shortcuts rather than human goals. We present HINT (Human-INTent INcepTion), an agentic framework inspired by the human manipulation principles: semantic intent changes sparsely at manipulation-pattern transitions, whereas continuous control primarily depends on the evolving object-hand relationship. HINT invokes semantic reasoning only at pattern transitions to resolve the current subtask and target, then maintains this commitment through multi-view grounding and visual tracking. We explore two visual interfaces-image-space semantic highlighting and attention-prior injection-to communicate the tracked intent to the action policy without introducing additional trainable parameters into the foundation action model. Experiments across three long-horizon tasks and out-of-distribution variants show that HINT substantially improves intent understanding, task progress, and end-to-end success across two foundation policies while preserving low-latency control.

AI.tldr: HINT (Human-INTent INcepTion) is an agentic framework that decouples sparse semantic intent reasoning from continuous visuomotor control, invoking high-level reasoning only at manipulation-pattern transitions and maintaining commitment via multi-view grounding and visual tracking. It injects tracked intent into the action policy through two trainable-free visual interfaces, improving intent understanding and task success across long-horizon manipulations.
AI.motivation: Current VLA models and action policies fail under dense, evolving visual inputs with sparse language guidance, as visual correlations dominate semantic intent and lead to visual shortcuts rather than goal-directed behavior. Real complex manipulations require selecting high-level intent at pattern transitions while continuously adapting to object-hand relationships.
AI.method: HINT is an agentic framework mirroring human manipulation principles: semantic intent is invoked sparsely only at manipulation-pattern transitions to resolve the subtask and target, after which this commitment is maintained through multi-view grounding and visual tracking. Two visual interfaces (image-space semantic highlighting and attention-prior injection) communicate the tracked intent to the action policy without adding trainable parameters to the foundation action model.
AI.result: Experiments across three long-horizon tasks and out-of-distribution variants show HINT substantially improves intent understanding, task progress, and end-to-end success across two foundation policies while preserving low-latency control.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling sparse semantic reasoning from continuous visuomotor control—aligned with human-like manipulation structure—effectively overcomes visual-shortcut bias in action policies, improving long-horizon manipulation performance without modifying or adding parameters to the underlying foundation model.

title: MASkills: Continual Skills Optimization for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems have shown strong performance on complex tasks, yet continual improvement from interaction experience remains challenging. Existing self-reflection methods build experience memories, but memories are mostly hard to invoke, refine, or scale, while agent skills offer a more actionable unit: structured procedural knowledge that specifies when to act, how to act, and which resources or tools to use. We introduce MASkills, a continual learning framework that optimizes multi-agent LLM systems through agent skills. MASkills presents a new agent-optimization pipeline that integrates skill-conditioned credit assignment, hierarchical credit aggregation, and momentum-smoothed optimization, enabling agent skill libraries to evolve through refinement, induction, consolidation, and pruning. Experiments on HotpotQA, LoCoMo, and GAIA demonstrate the effectiveness of MASkills across multiple agentic tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/DaRL-GenAI/MASkills

AI.tldr: MASkills is a continual learning framework for multi-agent LLM systems that optimizes agent skills (structured procedural knowledge) through a pipeline integrating skill-conditioned credit assignment, hierarchical credit aggregation, and momentum-smoothed optimization. It enables skill libraries to evolve via refinement, induction, consolidation, and pruning, showing effectiveness on HotpotQA, LoCoMo, and GAIA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-reflection methods build experience memories that are hard to invoke, refine, or scale. Agent skills offer a more actionable unit of structured procedural knowledge specifying when/how to act and which resources to use, enabling continual improvement from interaction experience.
AI.method: MASkills introduces an agent-optimization pipeline with three key components: (1) skill-conditioned credit assignment to attribute outcomes to relevant skills, (2) hierarchical credit aggregation to consolidate signals across levels, and (3) momentum-smoothed optimization for stable skill updates. The skill library evolves through four operations: refinement, induction, consolidation, and pruning.
AI.result: Experiments on HotpotQA, LoCoMo, and GAIA benchmarks demonstrate MASkills' effectiveness across multiple agentic tasks, showing that the continual learning framework with agent skills outperforms baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: MASkills provides a scalable and actionable continual learning paradigm for multi-agent LLM systems by treating agent skills as the core optimization unit, enabling structured evolution of procedural knowledge rather than relying on brittle memory-based self-reflection.

title: From Proxy Learning to Driving Decisions: A Transfer-Based Framework for Evaluating Future-Aware Autonomous Driving Planners
summary: Future-aware representations and world models are increasingly used in proposal-based autonomous-driving planners to improve trajectory selection. However, improvements in proxy objectives or restricted subsets are often interpreted as planning gains without verifying proposal ordering, selected trajectories, full-scale utility, and critical driving components. We propose the Proxy-to-Decision Transfer (PDT) Framework, an analysis framework that evaluates when learned future information supports a reliable driving-performance improvement claim. Its Decision-Transfer Decomposition Module localizes value loss through score margins, switch-conditioned utility, and support-versus-selection regret. Its Reliability-Constrained Validation Module requires exact pairing, a minimum meaningful effect, scale-expanded confirmation, safety non-compensation, sequential comparability, and family-level robustness. On a representative future-aware planner evaluated with NAVSIM-v1, component BCE decreases from 0.705 to 0.530 while held selected PDM decreases from 0.963 to 0.961. A separate candidate improves a 512-record prefix by 0.00909, with a scene-bootstrap 95% interval of [0.000744, 0.0177], but its 2048-record and complete-support intervals include zero. A proposal-level replay further confirms the switch-utility decomposition, yet none of 432 screened configurations passes the two-half, two-seed robustness gate. PDT therefore identifies where decision transfer fails or remains indeterminate across proxy, subset, aggregate, and selection evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Proxy-to-Decision Transfer (PDT) Framework, an analysis framework for evaluating when future-aware learned representations in autonomous-driving planners genuinely improve driving performance. The framework decomposes value loss through score margins, switch-conditioned utility, and support-versus-selection regret, and applies reliability constraints such as exact pairing and robustness testing. Empirical results show that proxy objective improvements (e.g., BCE dropping from 0.705 to 0.530) do not reliably translate to decision-level gains, with none of 432 screened configurations passing a robustness gate.
AI.motivation: The authors observe that proxy-objective improvements or restricted-subset gains in future-aware planners are often misinterpreted as genuine planning gains without verifying proposal ordering, selected-trajectory quality, full-scale utility, or critical driving components. This produces unreliable claims about learned future information improving driving performance.
AI.method: The PDT Framework consists of two modules: (1) a Decision-Transfer Decomposition Module that localizes value loss via score margins, switch-conditioned utility, and support-versus-selection regret; and (2) a Reliability-Constrained Validation Module requiring exact pairing, minimum meaningful effect, scale-expanded confirmation, safety non-compensation, sequential comparability, and family-level robustness.
AI.result: On NAVSIM-v1 with a future-aware planner, component BCE decreased from 0.705 to 0.530 while held-out selected PDM decreased only slightly from 0.963 to 0.961. A separate candidate improved a 512-record prefix by 0.00909 (bootstrap interval [0.000744, 0.0177]) but its larger-sample intervals included zero. Proposal-level replay confirmed the switch-utility decomposition, yet none of 432 screened configurations passed the two-half, two-seed robustness gate.
AI.conclusion: The PDT framework reveals where decision transfer fails or remains indeterminate across proxy, subset, aggregate, and selection evidence, demonstrating that proxy-objective gains do not reliably imply driving-performance improvements and highlighting the need for multi-level, robustness-constrained validation before claiming planning gains.

title: READY or Not: Reliable Enterprise Agent Deployment
summary: An AI agent can perform well on benchmarks and still be unsuitable for deployment. Existing AI-agent benchmarks measure whether an agent can complete realistic professional work, whereas enterprise deployment asks a different question: whether an agent can meet a required reliability level, under acceptable human oversight, and at tolerable cost. We introduce Reliable Enterprise Agent Deployment (READY), a framework for qualifying AI agents for deployment on enterprise workflows. READY preserves each workflow's own definition of successful execution while applying a common qualification procedure. Given an agent, a workflow, and a class of candidate oversight policies, READY measures the reliability and operating cost of the human-AI system, selects the minimum-cost policy that satisfies a specified reliability target, and statistically qualifies it on held-out cases. The resulting deployment profile characterizes the supported operating point: reliability, human-oversight burden, and cost. READY is implemented as an open testbed that decouples workflow specification, execution, evaluation, and qualification, and runs on existing agent-evaluation infrastructure. In an end-to-end clinical-audit case study spanning 16 agent systems and 750 cases, READY reveals differences hidden by autonomous performance: two systems separated by only 0.3 points in autonomous accuracy (72.8% vs. 72.5%) require 39.2% versus 29.6% human review, respectively, to qualify at the same 76% reliability target under the evaluated oversight policy. READY thus shifts enterprise agent evaluation from how well can the agent perform the work? to under what conditions, and at what cost, can it be reliably deployed? By making those conditions explicit and statistically testable, READY provides a basis for comparing agent systems, setting oversight requirements, and making evidence-based deployment decisions.

AI.tldr: READY is a framework for qualifying AI agents for enterprise deployment by measuring reliability, human oversight burden, and cost under candidate oversight policies, then statistically certifying the minimum-cost policy that meets a reliability target on held-out cases.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-agent benchmarks measure whether an agent can complete professional work autonomously, but enterprise deployment requires whether an agent can meet reliability levels under acceptable human oversight and tolerable cost—a fundamentally different qualification question that current benchmarks do not address.
AI.method: READY preserves each workflow's own success definition while applying a common qualification procedure: it measures reliability and operating cost of the human-AI system across a class of candidate oversight policies, selects the minimum-cost policy satisfying a specified reliability target, and statistically qualifies it on held-out cases. It is implemented as an open testbed that decouples workflow specification, execution, evaluation, and qualification, running on existing agent-evaluation infrastructure.
AI.result: In an end-to-end clinical-audit case study spanning 16 agent systems and 750 cases, READY revealed deployment differences hidden by autonomous performance: two systems separated by only 0.3 points in autonomous accuracy (72.8% vs. 72.5%) required 39.2% versus 29.6% human review to qualify at the same 76% reliability target.
AI.conclusion: READY shifts enterprise agent evaluation from "how well can the agent perform the work?" to "under what conditions, and at what cost, can it be reliably deployed?", providing a basis for comparing agents, setting oversight requirements, and making evidence-based deployment decisions.

title: Do Better Imagined Rollouts Mean Better Robot Control? A Controlled Study of World-Model Evaluation Under Feedback
summary: Predictive models are increasingly used in robotics for state estimation, planning, control, and policy evaluation, yet they are often judged by open-loop prediction accuracy over a fixed horizon. In closed-loop operation, a robot repeatedly acts, receives new measurements, updates its state estimate, and recomputes control. We study this difference in a differential-drive path-tracking task with biased odometry and intermittent landmark sensing. Six state estimators are evaluated across 24 sensing conditions using trajectory replay, a 20-step measurement-free rollout, and closed-loop tracking. Replay position RMSE correlates more strongly with closed-loop cross-track RMSE than rollout error (Spearman rho = 0.923 vs. 0.774) and selects a different estimator from the closed-loop optimum in 5/24 conditions, compared with 18/24 for the rollout metric. We then vary rollout horizon and measurement-update interval. With H=20, rank agreement decreases from rho = 0.916 with measurements at every step to rho = 0.774 with no measurements. A horizon-update grid shows that long prediction horizons remain informative when regular corrections are retained, whereas long rollouts without correction can produce rankings that differ substantially from closed-loop behavior. We also test recurrent estimators trained on longer sensing outages. This improves the EKF-anchored models under combined sensing degradation, reducing GRU-EKF cross-track RMSE from 1.72 m to 1.06 m, but the gain is not consistent across isolated outages or estimator architectures. These results show that predictive-model evaluation in robotics should specify both prediction horizon and measurement-update schedule. For models used in feedback, offline rollouts are most informative when their sensing and correction pattern reflects closed-loop operation. Code is available at https://github.com/rdharini2001/Robot_World_Model

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how predictive model evaluation metrics in robotics relate to actual closed-loop performance. Using a differential-drive path-tracking task with biased odometry and intermittent landmark sensing, the authors evaluate six state estimators across 24 sensing conditions. They find that trajectory replay position RMSE correlates more strongly with closed-loop cross-track RMSE than measurement-free rollouts, and that both prediction horizon and measurement-update schedule critically affect whether offline evaluation rankings match closed-loop behavior.
AI.motivation: Predictive models in robotics are typically judged by open-loop prediction accuracy over a fixed horizon, but in real closed-loop operation, robots repeatedly act, receive measurements, and update estimates. The authors aim to understand when and why offline evaluation metrics diverge from true closed-loop performance, and how evaluation protocols can be designed to better reflect real operating conditions.
AI.method: A differential-drive path-tracking task is used with biased odometry and intermittent landmark sensing. Six state estimators are evaluated across 24 sensing conditions using three protocols: trajectory replay, a 20-step measurement-free rollout, and closed-loop tracking. The authors analyze rank correlations between offline metrics and closed-loop cross-track RMSE, then systematically vary rollout horizon and measurement-update intervals. They also train recurrent estimators on longer sensing outages to assess generalization under degraded sensing.
AI.result: Replay position RMSE correlates more strongly with closed-loop cross-track RMSE than rollout error (Spearman rho = 0.923 vs. 0.774) and selects a different estimator from the closed-loop optimum in only 5/24 conditions vs. 18/24 for rollout. Rank agreement between rollout and closed-loop degrades from rho = 0.916 with every-step measurements to rho = 0.774 with no measurements at H=20. Long prediction horizons remain informative when corrections are retained. Training recurrent estimators on longer outages improved GRU-EKF cross-track RMSE from 1.72 m to 1.06 m under combined degradation, but gains were inconsistent across isolated outages or architectures.
AI.conclusion: Predictive-model evaluation in robotics should explicitly specify both prediction horizon and measurement-update schedule. Offline rollouts are most informative for feedback use when their sensing and correction pattern mirrors closed-loop operation. Model evaluation protocols must account for closed-loop dynamics rather than relying solely on open-loop prediction accuracy.

title: Semantic Signal-Assisted Inspection and Recovery Allocation in Reverse Logistics
comment: Accepted at the IEEE 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and Internet of Things (AIBThings 2026). 7 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/jiani19980225/ssads-reverse-logistics
summary: Reverse-logistics operators often decide how to inspect and route returned assets before their condition is fully observed, while full inspection consumes scarce labor. Semantic Signal-Assisted Decision Support converts return notes into a condition factor and a signal-quality score that guide inspection depth and recovery allocation under shared labor capacity. We evaluate the framework in three synthetic benchmark scenarios spanning information technology decommissioning, aircraft maintenance, and consumer-electronics returns. Across 30 paired simulation seeds, the keyword implementation improves net recovery value relative to a structured-feature comparator with noisy full inspection while reducing inspection cost in all three scenarios. A risk-blind comparator that skips inspection altogether still records higher value under the benchmark's purely economic objective. At matched inspection cost, score-guided targeting adds 53.9 thousand United States dollars per batch in the aircraft scenario but has little economic effect in the other two configurations; phrase and large language model extractors provide further gains in the aircraft scenario. These results show how narrative evidence can support inspection allocation before recovery decisions are made.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Semantic Signal-Assisted Decision Support, a framework that converts return notes into a condition factor and signal-quality score to guide inspection depth and recovery allocation under shared labor capacity in reverse logistics. Evaluated across three synthetic benchmark scenarios (IT decommissioning, aircraft maintenance, and consumer electronics returns), keyword-based extraction outperforms structured-feature comparators with noisy full inspection on net recovery value while reducing inspection cost. However, a risk-blind comparator skipping inspection achieves higher value under a purely economic objective. At matched inspection cost, score-guided targeting adds $53,900 per batch in the aircraft scenario, with phrase and LLM extractors yielding further gains.
AI.motivation: Reverse-logistics operators must make inspection and routing decisions about returned assets before their condition is fully known, yet full inspection consumes scarce labor. The paper motivates using narrative return notes as semantic evidence to support early decision-making under capacity constraints.
AI.method: The framework converts return notes into a condition factor and signal-quality score that guide (a) the depth of inspection and (b) recovery allocation while accounting for shared labor capacity. Three natural-language extractor implementations (keywords, phrases, large language models) are evaluated against structured-feature and risk-blind comparators across three synthetic benchmark scenarios with 30 paired simulation seeds.
AI.result: Keyword extraction improves net recovery value over a structured-feature comparator with noisy full inspection while reducing inspection cost in all three scenarios. Despite this, a risk-blind comparator skipping inspection records higher value under the purely economic objective. At matched inspection cost, score-guided targeting adds $53.9K per batch in the aircraft scenario but little economic effect elsewhere; phrase and LLM extractors provide additional aircraft-scenario gains.
AI.conclusion: Narrative evidence from return notes can meaningfully support inspection allocation before recovery decisions are made, though the economic benefit is scenario-dependent and sensitive to the objective function and the value of information relative to inspection cost.

title: Toward Robust LiDAR Semantic Segmentation for Real-World Deployment: Evaluation under Coarse Labels, Adverse Conditions, and Domain Shifts
summary: LiDAR-based semantic segmentation is a core perception module for autonomous vehicles and mobile robots. Despite the strong performance of recent state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks, existing evaluation protocols remain focused on clean, single-domain settings and fine-grained label taxonomies, leaving deployment readiness largely unassessed. Real-world systems must handle safety-critical label semantics, degraded sensing conditions, and cross-domain variability, yet no unified protocol currently addresses all three aspects together. In this paper, we propose a structured evaluation protocol that assesses the deployment readiness of LiDAR semantic segmentation models along three complementary dimensions: (i) coarse-label evaluation aligned with autonomous driving safety priorities, revealing how label granularity affects different methods; (ii) robustness under eight types of LiDAR corruptions designed to emulate real-world atmospheric, geometric, and sensor degradations; and (iii) domain generalization across datasets without adaptation. The evaluation includes inference speed measured on an embedded Jetson AGX Orin platform, directly reflecting deployment constraints. Our results show that fine-grained benchmark rankings do not always reflect safety-relevant performance, that all methods experience substantial degradation under corruptions with architecture-dependent robustness characteristics, and that current domain generalization remains insufficient for reliable deployment. These findings expose concrete gaps between benchmark performance and deployment readiness, and provide a reference protocol for more practically grounded evaluation of LiDAR semantic segmentation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a structured evaluation protocol for LiDAR semantic segmentation that assesses deployment readiness along three complementary dimensions: safety-aligned coarse-label evaluation, robustness under eight types of LiDAR corruptions, and cross-dataset domain generalization, with inference speed measured on an embedded Jetson AGX Orin platform. Results reveal that fine-grained benchmark rankings do not reflect safety-relevant performance, all methods degrade substantially under corruptions with architecture-dependent robustness, and domain generalization remains insufficient for reliable deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation protocols for LiDAR semantic segmentation focus on clean, single-domain settings with fine-grained label taxonomies, leaving deployment readiness unassessed. Real-world systems require simultaneous handling of safety-critical label semantics, degraded sensing conditions, and cross-domain variability, yet no unified protocol addresses all three aspects together.

Inference speed is additionally measured on an embedded Jetson AGX Orin platform to reflect deployment constraints.

Concrete gaps between benchmark performance and deployment readiness are exposed.

title: Beyond Context Windows: Persistent Discovery Context for Data-Centric Agents
summary: Data-centric agents repeatedly perform a discovery step before planning or execution: identifying the data objects relevant to a task. Yet successful discovery outcomes are typically discarded rather than reused. We introduce persistent discovery context, a lightweight memory layer that stores prior intent-to-object mappings and reuses them to augment future retrieval. Across three structured data environments, persistent discovery context consistently improves retrieval quality over metadata-only search, remains effective with automatically generated memories, and exposes a reproducible interference failure mode. In lexically sparse domains, memory-only retrieval can even outperform metadata-based retrieval. These findings suggest that discovery outcomes constitute a useful form of reusable context for data-centric agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces persistent discovery context, a lightweight memory layer for data-centric agents that stores and reuses prior intent-to-object mappings from previous discovery steps to augment future retrieval tasks, showing consistent retrieval quality improvements across structured data environments.
AI.motivation: Data-centric agents repeatedly discover data objects relevant to tasks before planning or execution, but these successful discovery outcomes are typically discarded rather than reused, representing wasted contextual information.
AI.method: The authors propose a lightweight memory layer called persistent discovery context that stores prior intent-to-object mappings from past discovery steps and reuses them to augment future retrieval queries.
AI.result: Across three structured data environments, persistent discovery context consistently improves retrieval quality over metadata-only search, remains effective with automatically generated memories, and exposes a reproducible interference failure mode. In lexically sparse domains, memory-only retrieval can outperform metadata-based retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Discovery outcomes constitute a useful form of reusable context for data-centric agents, warranting further exploration of memory-based retrieval augmentation in these systems.

title: Towards Trustworthy Autonomous Robots: An Explainable AI-Based Decision Framework
comment: 7 pages. Accepted version. Published in SoutheastCon 2026, IEEE, pp. 1-6
summary: Autonomous robots powered by deep learning face a fundamental auditability challenge: when incidents occur, investigators cannot reconstruct why the system made specific decisions. This paper presents TRACE (Transparent Reasoning Architecture for Credible Execution), a decision framework that ensures every autonomous action can be traced back to sensor evidence through documented causal chains. The framework organizes decision-making into four auditable layers: Semantic Perception for evidence-grounded entity recognition, Belief Reasoning for probabilistic state estimation with causal graphs, Action Synthesis for constraint-aware planning with counterfactual documentation, and Execution Verification for compliance monitoring. TRACE is model-agnostic yet designed to integrate learning-based perception modules (CNNs, transformers) while preserving decision-level auditability. We evaluate the framework using three objective metrics: Evidence Traceability (sensor-to-decision linkage), Decision Reconstructability (post-hoc analysis capability), and Temporal Continuity (audit trail completeness). Experimental evaluation on warehouse robot navigation demonstrates that TRACE achieves 98.6% evidence traceability, 99.0% temporal continuity, and 98.1% decision reconstructability across 500 simulated decision cycles. Post-hoc methods like LIME provide feature attributions but lack the artifact structure needed for decision-level reconstruction. The framework addresses EU AI Act requirements for high-risk system transparency and contributes to Explainable AI for safety-critical autonomous systems.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a four-layer decision framework (Semantic Perception, Belief Reasoning, Action Synthesis, Execution Verification) that enables full auditability of autonomous robot decisions by documenting causal chains from sensor evidence to actions. Evaluated on warehouse robot navigation, it achieves 98.6% evidence traceability, 99.0% temporal continuity, and 98.1% decision reconstructability across 500 simulated decision cycles.
AI.motivation: Autonomous robots powered by deep learning face a fundamental auditability challenge: when incidents occur, investigators cannot reconstruct why the system made specific decisions. Existing post-hoc methods like LIME provide feature attributions but lack the artifact structure needed for decision-level reconstruction.
AI.method: TRACE organizes decision-making into four auditable layers: (1) Semantic Perception for evidence-grounded entity recognition, (2) Belief Reasoning for probabilistic state estimation with causal graphs, (3) Action Synthesis for constraint-aware planning with counterfactual documentation, and (4) Execution Verification for compliance monitoring. The framework is model-agnostic yet integrates learning-based perception modules (CNNs, transformers) while preserving decision-level auditability.

AI.conclusion: TRACE addresses EU AI Act requirements for high-risk system transparency and contributes to Explainable AI for safety-critical autonomous systems by providing a structured artifact framework for decision-level reconstruction, surpassing feature-attribution-only approaches like LIME.

title: EmoStance: Response-Side Affective-Orientation Control for Empathetic Response Generation via Emoji Weak Supervision
comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP 2026
summary: Empathetic response generation requires models to decide not only what to say, but also how to respond to the previous speaker's affective situation. We formulate this as response-side affective-orientation control and use multi-annotator emoji distributions as weak affective--attitudinal evidence, rather than as output symbols or gold labels, to induce a latent control space that operationally approximates listener stance. We construct EmojiDialogue, an utterance-level extension of EmpatheticDialogues with emoji votes and confidence scores, and propose EmoStance, which models source-side affective expression, predicts a soft response-side orientation from dialogue context and speaker roles, and steers a frozen instruction-tuned LLM through continuous prefix embeddings. In blind pairwise evaluation with 20 annotators and 800 judgments, EmoStance achieves a 62.2% decisive win rate, with the clearest gains in contextual specificity and perceived responsiveness, while remaining complementary to external-knowledge methods. Code, annotation metadata, and reconstruction scripts are available in our GitHub repository: https://github.com/18277390221/EmoStance.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates empathetic response generation as response-side affective-orientation control, using multi-annotator emoji distributions as weak affective evidence to induce a latent control space approximating listener stance. It introduces EmojiDialogue (an utterance-level extension of EmpatheticDialogues with emoji votes and confidence scores) and EmoStance, which models source-side affect, predicts soft response-side orientation from context and speaker roles, and steers a frozen instruction-tuned LLM via continuous prefix embeddings. EmoStance achieves a 62.2% decisive win rate in blind pairwise evaluation with 20 annotators/800 judgments.
AI.motivation: Empathetic response generation needs control over both content and the affective orientation of the response toward the previous speaker's situation; existing work lacks explicit control over how to respond (listener stance).
AI.method: Constructs EmojiDialogue with multi-annotator emoji votes/confidence scores as weak evidence; proposes EmoStance which models source-side affective expression, predicts soft response-side orientation from dialogue context and speaker roles, and steers a frozen instruction-tuned LLM through continuous prefix embeddings.
AI.result: In blind pairwise evaluation with 20 annotators and 800 judgments, EmoStance achieves a 62.2% decisive win rate, with largest gains in contextual specificity and perceived responsiveness, and remains complementary to external-knowledge methods.
AI.conclusion: Emoji distributions serve as effective weak affective-attitudinal evidence for inducing a latent control space that approximates listener stance, improving empathetic response generation without relying on external knowledge.

title: FUSE: An Evaluating Framework for Dangerous Capabilities of LLMs
summary:
Fragmented safety evaluation undermines the governance of dangerous AI capabilities. We present a modular framework that evaluates each model through three orthogonal pipelines---Knowledge ($K$), Defense ($D$), and Harm ($H$)---under a unified protocol, aggregating results into a standardized dangerous-capability profile $φ$. Pluggable modules supply scenario seeds, knowledge banks, hazard queries, and judge rubrics, while the core evaluation engine remains unchanged across domains; the CB evaluation is complemented by a cyber pilot demonstrating protocol transfer.
  Instantiating the framework with a chemical-biological (CB) module, we evaluate 12 commercial LLMs from four families. Our first contribution is a horizontal comparison of dangerous capability across models and model families: the three dimensions expose sharply divergent profiles---models with comparable knowledge differ in refusal resilience, and strong defenders do not generate less harmful content when they do comply---while family-level patterns further separate Claude, DeepSeek, and GPT models. The second is a temporal analysis of capability evolution: tracking $K$, $D$, and $H$ against model release dates reveals that dangerous capability has not monotonically declined; newer models deepen knowledge while only partially improving defense, showing that scaling and alignment progress do not uniformly translate into safety. Reliability is established via cross-judge consistency (bootstrap $ρ> 0.79$, 4 of 5 judges) and pipeline orthogonality ($K$--$D$--$H$ inter-correlations $ρ\in [0.32, 0.52]$).

AI.tldr: Presents a modular framework for evaluating dangerous AI capabilities through three orthogonal pipelines—Knowledge (K), Defense (D), and Harm (H)—under a unified protocol, aggregated into a standardized dangerous-capability profile φ. Applied to 12 commercial LLMs across 4 families, revealing divergent capability profiles across models and families, non-monotonic capability evolution over time, and validated via cross-judge consistency and pipeline orthogonality.
AI.motivation: Fragmented safety evaluation undermines the governance of dangerous AI capabilities; a unified, modular evaluation framework is needed to enable systematic horizontal comparison and temporal tracking of dangerous capabilities.
AI.method: A modular framework with three orthogonal pipelines (Knowledge, Defense, Harm) under a unified protocol, using pluggable modules (scenario seeds, knowledge banks, hazard queries, judge rubrics) and a core evaluation engine. Instantiated with a chemical-biological (CB) module and a cyber pilot, applied to 12 commercial LLMs from 4 families with horizontal and temporal analyses.
AI.result: Models with comparable knowledge differ in refusal resilience; strong defenders do not generate less harmful content when complying. Family-level patterns distinguish Claude, DeepSeek, and GPT. Dangerous capability has not monotonically declined over release dates—newer models deepen knowledge while only partially improving defense. Reliability confirmed via bootstrap cross-judge consistency (ρ > 0.79, 4/5 judges) and pipeline orthogonality (inter-correlations ρ ∈ [0.32, 0.52]).
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a standardized dangerous-capability profile that enables meaningful cross-model and cross-time safety comparisons. Scaling and alignment progress do not uniformly translate into safety gains, motivating the need for continuous, modular dangerous-capability evaluation.

title: Examining the Vulnerability of Multi-Agent Medical Systems to Human Interventions for Clinical Reasoning
summary: Human interventions at fault points can alter the diagnostic accuracy of multi-agent medical systems. We defined fault points as moments in AI agent conversations, in which an agent's reasoning became most vulnerable to external influence. Using the MedQA dataset, this study analyzed simulated doctor-patient conversations to measure how interventions shifted reasoning and accuracy. Correct intervention methods showed an improvement in baseline diagnostic accuracy of up to 40%, while incorrect or bias-related interventions degraded performance by up to 6% and increased diagnostic drift and uncertainty. Beyond performance changes, our analysis revealed behavioral similarities between cognitive biases in simulated agent environments and real-world clinical practice. Examples included premature closure and susceptibility to misleading cues. Overall, these findings demonstrate that identifying and guiding fault points with human interventions may provide a mechanism for improving diagnostic robustness in multi-agent medical systems.

AI.tldr: This study investigates human interventions at critical moments ("fault points") in multi-agent medical AI conversations, finding that correct interventions can improve diagnostic accuracy by up to 40% while incorrect or biased interventions degrade performance by up to 6%, and revealing behavioral parallels between simulated agent biases and real clinical cognitive biases.
AI.motivation: To determine whether strategic human guidance at vulnerable moments in AI agent reasoning can improve diagnostic accuracy and robustness in multi-agent medical systems.
AI.method: Using the MedQA dataset, the authors simulated doctor-patient conversations between AI agents, identified fault points (moments where agent reasoning is most vulnerable to external influence), and measured how various human interventions at these points shifted diagnostic reasoning and accuracy.
AI.result: Correct interventions improved baseline diagnostic accuracy by up to 40%, while incorrect or bias-related interventions degraded performance by up to 6%, increasing diagnostic drift and uncertainty. The analysis also revealed behavioral similarities between cognitive biases in simulated agents and real-world clinical practice, including premature closure and susceptibility to misleading cues.
AI.conclusion: Identifying and guiding fault points through human interventions offers a promising mechanism for improving diagnostic robustness in multi-agent medical systems.

title: ASCII Attack: Recontextualising Harmful Requests as Artistic Critique in Large Language Models
summary: Safety alignment trains large language models to refuse harmful requests stated plainly, but that training is applied mostly to surface form. Requests that only recontextualise the same operational content, changing how the model reads it, are therefore only weakly covered. The ASCII Attack is one such recontextualisation. It is single-turn and black-box: one message, with no access to model internals. It embeds a fully legible harmful request in ASCIl-art characters, presents it as artwork, and asks for feedback. Unlike ArtPrompt, it hides nothing: the request stays readable. The reply is written as artistic critique and can contain operational detail that a plain request would have been refused for. Every framed prompt is paired with a direct-question control, so the contrast is isolated from topic, model and decoding variation. The contrast identifies a bundled surface, not one isolated channel. Across eleven models and eight harm topics, a harm-aware classifier judges 62% of framed prompts harmful against 42% of controls. On the most susceptible model the framed prompt succeeds 93% of the time. A single query matches or exceeds published single-query attacks under four of five harm judges. The effect tracks the model more than the topic and does not diminish with scale. At least one judge dissents from the panel majority on nearly two-thirds of framed rows, which is itself a measurement-validity finding. That pattern is consistent with mismatched generalisation.

AI.tldr: The ASCII Attack is a single-turn, black-box jailbreak that embeds a fully legible harmful request in ASCII-art characters and presents it as artwork for critique, bypassing safety alignment that only covers surface form. Across 11 models and 8 harm topics, 62% of framed prompts are judged harmful versus 42% of plain controls, demonstrating that recontextualisation alone—without hiding content—is sufficient to evade refusal training.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment trains models to refuse plainly stated harmful requests, but this training generalises poorly to recontextualised surfaces. The authors aim to demonstrate that a simple recontextualisation (presenting legible harmful content as ASCII art) can bypass alignment, highlighting a fundamental limitation of surface-level safety training.
AI.method: The attack embeds a readable harmful request in ASCII-art form, presents it as artwork, and asks for feedback, with replies framed as artistic critique. Each framed prompt is paired with a direct-question control to isolate the framing effect from topic/model/decoding variance. The attack is single-turn, black-box (no access to model internals), and unlike ArtPrompt, hides nothing—the request remains readable.
AI.result: Across 11 models and 8 harm topics, a harm-aware classifier judges 62% of framed prompts harmful versus 42% of controls. On the most susceptible model the framed prompt succeeds 93% of the time. A single query matches or exceeds published single-query attacks under four of five harm judges. The effect tracks the model more than the topic and does not diminish with scale. Nearly two-thirds of framed rows have at least one judge dissenting from the panel majority, indicating measurement-validity issues consistent with mismatched generalisation.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment is fragile to surface-level recontextualisation even when harmful content remains fully legible. The attack's effectiveness varies by model rather than topic and persists at scale, suggesting current alignment methods generalise poorly to novel framing. Notable disagreement among safety judges also raises questions about how harmfulness is measured in evaluation benchmarks.

title: PEARL: Path-Entity Aligned Relational Learning with Contextual Subgraphs for Inductive Knowledge Graph Completion
summary: Inductive knowledge graph completion (IKGC) aims to predict missing links involving entities unseen during training, requiring models to learn transferable relational and structural patterns. Existing subgraph- and path-based approaches often encode relational paths independently of their surrounding query subgraphs, although the predictive relevance of a path may vary across structural contexts. We propose PEARL, a Path-Entity Aligned Relational Learning framework that models paths as context-conditioned reasoning signals. PEARL constructs a query-specific contextual subgraph from the union of the query entities' neighborhoods and uses a large language model (LLM)-guided retriever to distill semantically relevant paths. It then builds a bipartite interaction graph over paths, contextual entities, and a global subgraph representation, allowing path embeddings to adapt to local and global structural evidence. To suppress noise introduced by the enlarged context, PEARL employs a dual-view contrastive objective that promotes representation consistency under stochastic contextual perturbations. Experiments on WN18RR, FB15k-237, and NELL-995 show that PEARL obtains the best average Hits@10 among the compared IKGC methods on all three benchmarks. Ablation studies, efficiency analyses, and case studies further validate the contributions of contextual subgraph modeling, semantic path retrieval, path-entity interaction, and contrastive regularization.

AI.tldr: PEARL is a framework for inductive knowledge graph completion that models paths as context-conditioned reasoning signals, using LLM-guided path retrieval, bipartite path-entity interaction graphs, and dual-view contrastive learning to achieve state-of-the-art Hits@10 on WN18RR, FB15k-237, and NELL-995.
AI.motivation: Existing subgraph- and path-based IKGC approaches encode relational paths independently of their surrounding query subgraphs, overlooking the fact that the predictive relevance of a path may vary across different structural contexts. This motivates modeling paths as context-conditioned reasoning signals rather than static features.
AI.method: PEARL constructs a query-specific contextual subgraph by taking the union of query entities' neighborhoods. It uses an LLM-guided retriever to distill semantically relevant paths, then builds a bipartite interaction graph over paths, contextual entities, and a global subgraph representation so that path embeddings adapt to both local and global structural evidence. A dual-view contrastive objective promotes representation consistency under stochastic contextual perturbations to suppress noise from the enlarged context.
AI.result: On WN18RR, FB15k-237, and NELL-995, PEARL achieves the best average Hits@10 among compared IKGC methods across all three benchmarks. Ablation studies, efficiency analyses, and case studies validate the contributions of each component including contextual subgraph modeling, semantic path retrieval, path-entity interaction, and contrastive regularization.
AI.conclusion: PEARL demonstrates that treating paths as context-conditioned reasoning signals—rather than capturing them independently—substantially improves inductive knowledge graph completion, with each designed component (contextual subgraph, semantic retrieval, bipartite interaction, contrastive regularization) contributing to overall performance.

title: SkillGLoW: Procedural-Family Skill Consolidation for Self-Improving Agents on Long-Horizon Task Streams
summary: LLM agents increasingly self-improve by writing and reusing textual skills, kept either as one global document or as a flat pool of per-task entries, though most of the evidence comes from domains with structurally similar tasks. On long-horizon workloads where each task demands a different solution, the two forms fail in opposite ways: the document collapses into generic discipline, while the pool inflates and its entries stay bound to the instance that wrote them. We argue the missing unit of reuse is the solving procedure shared by a cluster of related tasks, and build SkillGLoW (Global-Local Weave) around it: the local skills a task writes from its own execution are aggregated into procedural families and compressed into de-instantiated global priors, while the instance detail they hold is regenerated per task rather than stored; a commit gate admits a prior only when real execution shows it does not degrade the deployed library. Across four benchmarks (mathematical reasoning, terminal automation, software repair, and embodied control) and three models, the priors gain 17.2 points (hard) over the no-skill baseline on average, with positive gains in all 12 continual-improvement runs, and 18.0 with local regeneration, while the library holds one prior per procedural family, 3.6x more compact than the per-task pool. Under the same protocol GLoW leads a published single-document optimizer on 15 of 21 cells. Unmodified, the library lifts success on unseen ALFWorld tasks from 73.9% to 83.9%, evidence that what transfers is procedure rather than task memory.

AI.tldr: SkillGLoW (Global-Local Weave) is a procedural skill-reuse framework for LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Instead of storing skills globally (which collapses into generic text) or per-task (which inflates and overfits), it clusters local execution-derived skills into procedural families, compresses them into de-instantiated global priors, and regenerates instance-specific details per task at inference time. A commit gate only admits priors validated by real execution. Across four benchmarks and three models, it improves hard-task success by 17.2 points over a no-skill baseline (18.0 with local regeneration), holds one prior per family (3.6x more compact than per-task pools), and transfers procedure rather than task memory (unseen ALFWorld success rises from 73.9% to 83.9%).
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent skill-reuse systems use either a single global document or a flat per-task pool. On long-horizon workloads where tasks are structurally diverse, the global document degenerates into generic advice while the per-task pool becomes bloated and instance-bound. Neither captures the solving procedure shared by clusters of related tasks, which is the correct reusable unit.
AI.method: SkillGLoW defines "procedural families" as clusters of related tasks sharing a solving procedure. Local skills from a task's execution are aggregated into these families, then compressed into de-instantiated global priors (removing instance-specific details). At inference, instance detail is regenerated per task rather than stored. A commit gate admits a prior into the deployed library only when real execution demonstrates it does not degrade performance.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks (mathematical reasoning, terminal automation, software repair, embodied control) and three models, priors yield +17.2 hard-task points over the no-skill baseline on average (positive gains in all 12 continual-improvement runs), or +18.0 with local regeneration. The library maintains one prior per family, 3.6x more compact than a per-task pool. GLoW outperforms a published single-document optimizer on 15/21 cells. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, the unmodified library lifts success from 73.9% to 83.9%.
AI.conclusion: The discovered transferable unit for long-horizon LLM agents is the shared solving procedure across a cluster of tasks, not generic global advice or per-task memory. SkillGLoW demonstrates that de-instantiating procedural priors and regenerating instance detail per task yields compact, generalizable skill libraries that improve performance and transfer to unseen tasks—evidence that what transfers is procedure rather than task memory.

title: PhoenixNest-Video: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Agent Framework for Automated Video Interview Assessment
summary: Interview assessment requires per-criterion judgments grounded in behavioral evidence, yet surging applicant volumes have made human-only evaluation costly and inconsistent, while existing AI approaches yield opaque scores without traceable rationale. We introduce PhoenixNest-Video, an evidence-grounded multimodal agent framework for automated video interview assessment. It builds a semantic video graph as structured working memory, performs rubric-conditioned retrieval with cross-modal verification across visual, audio, and textual streams, and produces per-criterion scores anchored to the candidate's materials. A Scorer trained via Rubrics-based Reinforcement Learning with dual rewards for rubric alignment and score-level differentiation internalizes the discriminative structure of multi-level rubrics. PhoenixNest-Video attains 91.50\% grade-level accuracy on VInterview-2025, outperforming substantially larger proprietary models. A compact, rubric-grounded agent therefore scores candidates in closer agreement with an expert panel than direct prompting of much larger models, and exposes the evidence behind each score for human review.

AI.tldr: PhoenixNest-Video is an evidence-grounded multimodal agent framework for automated video interview assessment. It builds a semantic video graph as structured working memory, performs rubric-conditioned retrieval with cross-modal verification, and produces per-criterion scores with traceable evidence. A Scorer trained via Rubrics-based Reinforcement Learning with dual rewards achieves 91.50% grade-level accuracy on VInterview-2025, outperforming much larger proprietary models while exposing score rationale for human review.
AI.motivation: Human-only evaluation of interviews is costly and inconsistent due to surging applicant volumes, while existing AI approaches generate opaque scores without traceable, evidence-grounded rationale for per-criterion judgments.
AI.method: The framework (1) builds a semantic video graph as structured working memory from video data, (2) performs rubric-conditioned retrieval with cross-modal verification across visual, audio, and textual streams, and (3) produces per-criterion scores anchored to candidate materials. A Scorer is trained via Rubrics-based Reinforcement Learning with dual rewards for rubric alignment and score-level differentiation, internalizing the discriminative structure of multi-level rubrics.
AI.result: PhoenixNest-Video achieves 91.50% grade-level accuracy on the VInterview-2025 benchmark, outperforming substantially larger proprietary models in agreement with an expert panel.
AI.conclusion: A compact, rubric-grounded agent can score candidates in closer agreement with an expert panel than direct prompting of much larger models, while exposing the evidence behind each score for transparent human review.

title: PGPO: Potential-Guided Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic Tasks
summary: Group-based reinforcement learning (RL) has become an effective paradigm for LLM post-training, but in multi-turn agentic tasks with sparse terminal rewards, it often provides coarse credit for intermediate actions. To obtain more fine-grained credit assignment, recent work such as GiGPO introduces step-level advantages for intermediate actions. However, these step-level signals still rely on the final outcome of each individual trajectory. As a result, actions within failed trajectories can remain poorly differentiated, so effective actions can receive the same unfavorable credit as erroneous ones. In this work, we propose Potential-Guided Policy Optimization (PGPO) for multi-turn agentic tasks. PGPO estimates empirical state potentials from anchor-state-group return statistics within each rollout group. It then derives action advantages from potential differences between adjacent states, enabling cross-trajectory credit propagation. This provides finer-grained step-level credit assignment, especially within failed trajectories. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show strong overall performance relative to recent group-based RL methods. Further analysis provides evidence that PGPO yields more informative failure-side credit signals with negligible training overhead.

AI.tldr: PGPO (Potential-Guided Policy Optimization) improves fine-grained credit assignment in multi-turn agentic RL by estimating empirical state potentials from anchor-state-group return statistics and deriving action advantages from potential differences between adjacent states, enabling cross-trajectory credit propagation especially within failed trajectories.
AI.motivation: Group-based RL for LLM post-training provides coarse credit in multi-turn agentic tasks with sparse terminal rewards. Existing step-level methods like GiGPO still rely on final outcomes of individual trajectories, leaving actions within failed trajectories poorly differentiated.
AI.method: PGPO estimates empirical state potentials from anchor-state-group return statistics within each rollout group, then derives action advantages from potential differences between adjacent states, enabling cross-trajectory credit propagation for finer-grained step-level credit assignment.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show strong overall performance relative to recent group-based RL methods, with more informative failure-side credit signals and negligible training overhead.
AI.conclusion: PGPO provides finer-grained step-level credit assignment, particularly within failed trajectories, effectively addressing the limitations of prior group-based RL approaches during LLM post-training.

title: Propose to Learn, Learn to Propose: Evaluability-Aware Assistance under Bounded Rationality
summary: AI assistants often collaborate by proposing candidate edits, plans, or designs that users evaluate before adoption. Existing assistance methods focus on proposal quality or user-goal inference, often assuming that the user can reliably evaluate any proposal, which can fail in practice because of bounded rationality. We study evaluability-aware proposal planning, where proposals serve both as task interventions and as probes for learning latent preferences and evaluation constraints, where the resulting belief updates then guide later proposals. We formalise this setting as ProSE, a hidden-parameter sequential assistance problem, and instantiate it with a KL-regularised bounded-rational binary response model in which acceptance trades off value gain against a distance-dependent evaluability penalty. Analysing the planning consequence of this likelihood reveals that likely accepted proposals and informative probes need not coincide, which explains why planners that only pursue acceptance systematically underperform. We operationalise ProSE with \textsc{ProSE-Plan}, a depth-2 Bayes-adaptive planner that scores proposals by possible responses and response-induced posterior beliefs. In controlled graph simulations, \textsc{ProSE-Plan} improves over evaluability-unaware and myopic baselines when evaluation cost is the bottleneck, and a probe-commit ablation confirms that our approach selects informative proposals that simpler methods miss. Our results thus identify user evaluability as a planning-relevant dimension of AI assistance, complementary to generation quality and preference inference.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces evaluability-aware proposal planning (ProSE), a framework where AI assistant proposals serve dual purposes: task interventions and probes for learning latent user preferences and evaluation constraints. A depth-2 Bayes-adaptive planner (ProSE-Plan) improves performance when evaluation cost is a bottleneck, outperforming evaluability-unaware and myopic baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing AI assistance methods focus on proposal quality or user-goal inference but assume users can reliably evaluate any proposal—an assumption that fails under bounded rationality. The paper identifies that proposals should also serve as probes to learn latent preferences and evaluation constraints, a dimension overlooked by prior work.
AI.method: Formalizes evaluability-aware proposal planning as ProSE, a hidden-parameter sequential assistance problem instantiated with a KL-regularised bounded-rational binary response model. Acceptance trades off value gain against a distance-dependent evaluability penalty. Introduces ProSE-Plan, a depth-2 Bayes-adaptive planner that scores proposals by possible responses and response-induced posterior beliefs.
AI.result: Analyzing the likelihood reveals that likely-accepted proposals and informative probes need not coincide, explaining why acceptance-only planners systematically underperform. In controlled graph simulations, ProSE-Plan improves over evaluability-unaware and myopic baselines when evaluation cost is the bottleneck. A probe-commit ablation confirms the approach selects informative proposals that simpler methods miss.
AI.conclusion: User evaluability is a planning-relevant dimension of AI assistance, complementary to generation quality and preference inference. The work establishes that adapting proposals with respect to evaluation constraints can lead to better overall assistance outcomes.

title: Task-Level Natural Language Priors as Learning Signals for Low-Resource LLM Training
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often struggle when low-resource training data are ambiguous or incomplete. Task-level natural-language priors can provide useful guidance in such settings, but existing approaches usually treat these priors as input context rather than as learning signals during training. We propose Prior-Guided Tuning (PGT), a training perspective that incorporates natural-language priors as auxiliary learning signals for low-resource LLM training. Under this perspective, we introduce Contrastive Prior Steering (CPS), which keeps the original supervised objective intact while adding positive and negative prior-conditioned auxiliary losses to encourage task-consistent learning and discourage plausible but misleading alternatives. Experiments on AmbiMath, Jigsaw, and MNLI/HANS show that CPS consistently improves over plain and prompt fine-tuning. On AmbiMath, CPS achieves 97.6% average exact-match accuracy. On Jigsaw, CPS improves average Macro F1 by 9.5 percentage points over standard fine-tuning, and with 1/10 of the experimental training data slightly exceeds full-data plain fine-tuning. On HANS, CPS improves non-entailment accuracy by 8.3 and 5.2 percentage points for LLaMA 3.1 8B and Qwen 2.5 7B, respectively, while maintaining comparable in-domain MNLI accuracy. These results support our central claim: task-level natural-language priors can provide useful guidance as auxiliary learning signals for low-resource LLM training. Our code and data will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Prior-Guided Tuning (PGT), a training perspective that uses task-level natural-language priors as auxiliary learning signals (not just input context) for low-resource LLM training. It introduces Contrastive Prior Steering (CPS), which adds positive and negative prior-conditioned auxiliary losses alongside the supervised objective. Experiments on AmbiMath, Jigsaw, and MNLI/HANS show consistent improvements over standard fine-tuning, with notable gains on low-resource benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with low-resource training data that is ambiguous or incomplete. Existing approaches treat task-level natural-language priors merely as input context rather than as learning signals during training, leaving valuable guidance underutilized.
AI.method: The proposed approach, Prior-Guided Tuning (PGT), frames natural-language priors as auxiliary learning signals. Within this framework, Contrastive Prior Steering (CPS) keeps the original supervised objective intact while adding positive prior-conditioned auxiliary losses (to encourage task-consistent learning) and negative prior-conditioned losses (to discourage plausible but misleading alternatives).
AI.result: CPS consistently outperforms plain and prompt fine-tuning. On AmbiMath it reaches 97.6% average exact-match accuracy. On Jigsaw, it improves Macro F1 by 9.5 percentage points over standard fine-tuning, and with 1/10 of the data slightly exceeds full-data plain fine-tuning. On HANS, non-entailment accuracy improves by 8.3 and 5.2 percentage points for LLaMA 3.1 8B and Qwen 2.5 7B while maintaining in-domain MNLI accuracy.
